For years, whenever my Customers have asked me for a Mild Tea, I have advised the Pure. old Fashioned China which I keep, and the advice has been appreciated. It is very satisfactory to them tint such an eminent authority as Sir Andrew Clarke, the London Physician, corroborates opinion. Here is an extract from an interesting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day, to the Students of the London Hospital: 'Tea is a blessed beverage. Ido not know what I should do without it. But there is tea and tea, and one of the teas I have in my mind is the representation of all that is physiologically wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions here and there, and about five o'clock, when I get into a place, the lady of the house will say to me : ' Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let me give you a cup ot tea,' I say 'thank you very much. But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew. and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a cup and fills thecup up with water. Now I call it positivecruelty to give Unlike that to anybody and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. Tea, to be useful, should be first of an Black China Tea ; the Indian Tea which is being cultivated has become so powertul in its effects upon the nervous system that a cup of it taken early in the morning, as many do. SO disorders the nervous system that those who take it actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and It produces a form of nervous diSturbance, which is most painful to witness. If you want to have, either for yourselves or for your patients, tea which will not injure and which will refresh, get Black China Tea, putting in the right measure—the old fashioned teaspoonful for each person and one for the blessed pot. Then pour on briskly boiling water, and within five minutes you must pour It off again, or it will become wicked instead of good." Such is Sir Andrew Clarke's opinion and advise. A few words of warning, however, are necessary to those who have for goiten what this old fashioned tea is like.' The colour of the tea after Ma brewed will be found tobe much paler than that now in use, and the taste may not be acceptable at first owing to its apparent insipidness ; but if its use is persisted in, it will very soon be found to be much more suitable for the system. and it, in a week to two after Its use, a trial is again made of the kind now in ordinary use, you , will wonder however you could have been using Maud you will endorse Sir Andrew's statement. Thb first consignment of fresh salmon from British Colunibia to Europe, which consisted ,of thirty tbousand,pounds from the Fraser liver,left New York the other day for Hamburg in the cold- storage compartment of a German steamer. Frozen salmon from Canada has often been sent to Eng- land. but this is ,the first cargo from the Pacific coast, and if the -experiment proves successful, a very large trade ,will result. The rivers of ikitish Columbia yielded nearly eleven million pounds of salmon during a 8,31, although it was regarded as a bad year.

The last week's death rate shows with terrible distinctness what a deadly plague is raging among us. The London death-rate is up to forty, which means more than two deaths for every one at the normal rate, and there is no room this time to ex- plain away the 'figures by any exceptional cireum- stances other than-disease. For the great towns the death-rate stands at thirty-three, far above the usual average, but-this gives no idea of the mortality in some places—as,,for instance Portsmouth, wheie the deaths have been at the rate of fifty-seven per thousand.

The change which has takemplace in the position of Prince George will greatly affect his future employments and pursuits. ;His active naval career may be regarded as over. it will he impossible for him now to remain in active service, and to take the regular duties of a naval officer. He may, and no doubt will, still remain in the service, but he must merge the naval in the ,newer and more dis- tinguished duties to which ihe has been called. As the next heir to the Crown he will have to spend most of his time in this country, and • take up the duties which were being discharged by the Duke of Clarence. More than ever the rrince of Wales needs an assistant in the dignified social and, ceremonial functions which he performs, and this, position will naturally fall to Prince George. At a very early date he will take his seat in the,House of Lords, with the title, probably, of Duke oflient,nd all his, future occupations must be •regulated.by the fact that he stands next to his fatherin succession to the Crown.

A meeting of the Irish Nationalist party will be held immediately before the opening of the Anew session. Its, first business will be to elect a sessional chairman, and, since Mr, Justin M'Carthy is stead- fast in his request to be released from a position which entails upon him much personal sacritioe, Mr. .John Dillon will be asked to succeed him. _A proposition will. I understand, be submitted that Mr. Dillon shall, be assisted in the discharge of his duties tby a small committee of members of the party. The carrying out of this an angement will complete an unprezedimted occurrence in the House of Commons. Of the several leaders of party or sections of party who were in the House when the session closed only one, and he the oldest in point of years, will return to his place. In the room of Mr. Smith will be Mr. Balfour. Mr. Chamberlain succeeds Lord Hartingtoil, Mr. Dillon Mr. Justin M'Carthy, and of last year's leaders only Mr. Glad- stone will remain.

Big Ben is aboatto be ()Mused by Great Paul. After much consideration of plans, says "The Building News," the Dean and Chapter have jest commissioned Messrs. John Smith and Sons, Derby, the well-known cloekmakers, to make a new clock ' to replace the old one in the south-west tower of the Cathedral. The old clock strikes the hours on the old "Phelps" bell, but the new one will strike upon "Great Paul,' which is nearly seventeen tons weight, with a hamar weighing 6801 b. The quatter-chimes will be struck ,muoft the same as before, but provision will be made kti the clock so that chimes on four bells may be added at a future time. The two dials, which are 16ft.diameter, will be unaltered, except that the central part will be arranged for illumination at night. The clock inaovement will be a very large piece of machinery, ,designed by Lord Grimthorpe. and it is guaranteed Dlessrs. Smith and Sons to keep time with very great accuracy. There will be special precision apparatus, whereby the first blow of the hours will fall within one se,:ond of Greenwich time, and the first blow of the three-quarters will also strike with the saute accuracy. Some idea of the great size of this clock may be formed when it is known that the hammer which strikes the bell is 6601b.' while the hammer which strikes" Big Ben" at the Rouses of Parliament is about 4501 b.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY- 23 1892. DOCTORED BY THE KING. ICA.NON EYRE ON ST. HELENS. From " Little Folks." "As fat as the Abbott of Waltham" was a proverb through the whole district around Waltham Abbey in the days of King Henry VIII. of England; and certainly the abbot might well be fat considering what a huge dinner he ate every day, and what rich dishes were served at it. Even when he began to suffer from indigestion and to corollain that ha was losing his appetite, it never occurred to him to leave off his habit of feeding on these unwholesome dainties.; and so, of course, he kept on getting worse and worse every day, till at last he 'came down to ckicken broth and light bread-cakes, and could hardly manage even them. Now it happened that one morning a man in the rich uniform of the king's " Yeomen of the Guard" presented himself at the abbey gate; and the abbot's servants, delighted at such a chance of getting all the latest news from London, and hearing something about the -king himself and the ways of his palace, brought him into the great kitchen, and were -juet going to entertain him after the fashion of that hospittible age—which consisted in giving to every guest more to eat than he could possibly swallow—when the abbot, having heard of his coming and thinking-that he would like to hove a talk with the man trimself, gave orders to 'seed him,np. In he -came—a t'fine stalwart fellow, taller by 'nearly half a head than the biggest man in the ;household, and almost asehroad and bulky as the 'corpulent abbot •himself. 'His face (which was very' handsome, and marked with the bold, bluff, fearless 'look of man-who felt kimself equal to any diffi- culty or danger that might come in his way) seemed -strangely familiar to the churchman, who, however, tried in vain to,-call tomeind where and how he could have-seen it' before. , But-their talkladknot, proceeded far when the hour struck at which the poor old abbot made his daily pretence (forit•vms nothing better) of a mid- daymeal ; and so-he-invited the yeoman to eat with him. '"That will-I do 'gladly," said the guardsman.; "for I have heard men say that your lordship keepeth goodly cheer." '"Little doth that profit me since I cannot eat of it myself,' said the abbot, with a poen ; " bat me- thinks his Grace dling Henry must make better cheer than-1, if all the yeomen of his guard be as' well fed as thou art." The big guardsmen smiled:as if at a high compli-; ment, and they went down into the great hall for 1 to dinner, where the guest made such havoc -of a ' huge surloin of roast beef that the abbot—who had with difficulty4managed to swallow a few spoonfulel of his chicken-broth—looked on at his performance with mingled envy and amazement. " Truly thoushast a noble appetite, good fellow,' I -said heewatching his guest admiringly as the latter 'helped himself, again and again. "In truth, I would .gladly,pay a hundred pounds to be able to eat good beef as heartily as thou hest done, instead of peck- dug like a sparrow at such scraps as I have here." " Say!st thou so, Lord Abbot ?" replied the -yea- -man, with -a =very curious smile." " Methinks, If Ithat beall thy trouble, it may well be cured. There tie-now at tbo•Court an exceeding skilful physician, ,and such a feeas a hundred pounds might move him to take younlordship's case in hand." He laughed-in a somewhat strange way as he -spoke the last words; and the worthy abbot—whci felt that he was being made fun of, though he could not tell how-i-looked rather offended. But at the time he thought little more of it, though he had goodtcause toeremember it later on. 'Not long after the guardsman's visit to Waltham Abbey, the abbot suddenly received a summons to, come to London to present himself at Court, which he lost no time in doing, taking it for granted that thegreaeConrt-physician of whom his guest had told him must-have heard of his case, and wished to, treehis handeon him. In fancy he already found himself cured. and all the way to town he rejoiced, in the thought-of being able ere long to eat as mach EIS aver. :But from these bright visions he was doomed -to •be speedily and -very roughly awakened. Scarcely hadebe reached the gate of the palace, with his long' train of attendants behind him, and announced.himself with great dignity as" the lord Abbot-of ,Waltham," when a tall stern-looking man, whose rich dress, and massive gold chain showed him to be an officer of high rank in the royal house- hold, stepped forward with two stout yeomen at his ' backeand,.laying his hand on the shoulder of the amazed,churchman. said solemnly— " Abbot of Waltham, I arrest thee in the king's -name'!" Arrest,met.' cried the dismayed abbot. " What have I done.?" " That thou doubtless know'st better than I;" said the official, in a tone which seemed to imply that he gave the abbot credit for any crime on earth. "Away with him, guards, and bear him straight to the Tower?' At that awful name the poor abbot's heart sank down intotis boots; for he knew that the Tower of London was reserved for prisoners accused of high treason, and that the punishment of high treason was eieatle. and,although Henry VIII, has not yet, taken to beheading his queens and courtiers, he had done quite enongh to show that he cared nothing for any law but that of his own will and pleasuie. But what wrong could ills have ever committed? He had alwaysbeen a loyal subject—unless, indeed, it was high treaaon to have made one of the royal yeomen eattoo,much ; but surely the king would not behead hini,for that? At all tevents,)he was not doomed to instant execu- tion; for, on reaching the Tower, his guards led him into a cell, Which, being larger and more comfortable than he had expected, seemed to him a good sign. But it his -lodging was satisfactory, his board was not; for the-prison bill of fare consisted simply of dry breadand cold water, and not too much of either. After three •or four weeks .of this fare (which wonderfully toned down tha abbot's corpulent I frame), the same officer and the same guards who had brought him there entered his cell one morning, and bade him -follow them. He did so ruefully enough, thinking he-was being led out to execution; but instead of an axe and a block, or instruments of torture, the room into which they led him contained nothing worse than a ,fine piece of smoking roast beef, from which he was bidden to help himself. His lordship did not--wait to be asked twice, for his bread-and-water discipline bad bsought back his lost appetite surprisingly; and it was nearly half- an-hour ere he at last gave in, saying, 'with a deep grunt of enjoyment— "Never even in any youth, did I eat like this !" ",Pay me my hundred-pounds, then, for thou art cured," said a deep voice ;and turning with a start, he saw beside him a man whom he recognised at once as the king himself'! " Was it, then, your -Grace who Came to me as a yeoman ?" cried the Startled abbot. "I myself," said HenryIVIII, laughing ; "and in thanks for that good olieer4 breve cured thee, where- fore pay me my fee 1" The abbot paid, and was at once set free, glad to get off so easily. But the strange prescription turned out to be worth the money, after all; for from that day forth he amended his way of life, and his health was all the better for it in consequence. Deven ;KEIL

Though the Rev. Canon Eyre is at present rector of St. Peter's, Tiverton, four or five years work in St. Helens peculiarly fitted him for an advocate of the claims of our great populous centres to further ministerial aid, and this no doubt led to his being asked to visit Torquay the other night as a deputa- tion on beh alt of the 'Church Pastoral Aid Society, -to. plead thocause of Home Missions. - He preached 1 sermons on behalf ,of the Society at Ellacombe, on the Sunday, and on the Monday evening he spoke at &meeting at Elktconibe Parish rooms. In the c muse of his address Canon Eyre, speaking of St. Helene, where he had held a living immedi- ately before coming to Devonshire, amused his audience ley the description of the pungent smells which were so strongly in evidence there, and which were-so abominable that they baffled descrip- tion. They wrre produced by the manufacture of sialpiruretterNlydrogen, which emitted a smell very much like rotten eggs, but whilst these fumes were , fatal to vegetable life,and they saw all around trees without leaves, and' fields without grass, experts considered that they were not injurious to animal life-; certainly they did not affect hie health, and the death rate was not exceptionally high. The stone •of the churches and public buildings was turned black by these fumes, and the water in the .canal, by reason of themanufacturers turning their waste water into it, was of the consistency and •colour of pea soup, though it occasionally changed its colour when some different chemical was turned ointo it. He was really not exaggerating when he said that a visitor to St. Helens might, two minutes after leaving the station, imagine he was looking upon Pandemonium, for he would see ' men nearly naked, having only so much cloth- ing asddecency demanded, running out from the glasshouses carrying in their hands -long black rods at the end of which were large balls of fire, the black rod being the blow pipe and the ball of fire glass in a molten state. At Messrs.

irilkington's 'Works 3,000 men were employed, and Canon Eyre referred to the danger to life and limb to which these, and the men working at the manufacture of chemicals, were exposed, by reason of the nature of their avocation. He spoke of the great success attending a mission conducted in St. Helens, in which he took part, and amusingly des- cribed how he had literally compelled men to come in.' He said the amount of alcohol drinking amongst the colliers and others was beyond concep- tion, at the same time admitting the very great
temptation to which they were su—'bjected through exhaustion, brought about by working in terrible heat. It was absolutely impossible for clergymen

„.. and others to work in such a placo by suggesting any half measures in regard to total abstinence. He observed that when he came away from St. Helens he left there a Bible class of 770 men, and on his departure he had to shake hands with 565 of them the remainder being at their work, and as those from whom he was taking his leave could not say anything they put what they felt into the grip, with the result that his arm ached for three weeks afterwards. When he remembered the working-men in Lancashire getting their 3Gs., 408.. 505.. or 60s. a week, he pitied the poor Devonshire labourers with their 15s. a week, and. wondered how they lived. In Tiverton, where he now lived, the curse of the drink was committing dreadful ravages. There was a drink, skeleton in nearly every family. He had been there only fifteen months and the number of deaths from drink which he had heard of in that time was astounding. In Tiverton they _generally drank beer, but in St. Helens they drank rum, large quantities of it, and the special evil of •drinking spirits was that, instead of getting into a 'maudlin, good tempered, stupid state, the men who , gave way to it became perfect devils—he used the word deliberately. In conclusion, Canon Eyre be- -sought the sympathies and prayers of his audience on behalf of the Church Pastoral Aid Society.

div.head: RAIN-MAKING EXPERIMENTS.
div.p: RAIN-MAKING EXPERIMENTS.

The new science and art of " rain-making " does not appear to make much progress in India, and unfortunately this is one of those countries where the power to procure rain at will would be particu- larly valuable. At Bijapur, in the Bombay Pre- sidency, newly half a ton of dynamite has been ex- ,ploded on elevated around; but unhappily all this disturbance left the district just as dry as before. A -second discharge was then tried upon a flat-topped bill two hundred feet in height; but still not a .drop of fain. •-In Burma the conditions were con- sidered more favourable; but it happened that just ,when the Deputy-Commissioner and an assistant- engineer had got all ready for a tremendous explo- •sson down came the rain. The experiment, it is Added, was carried on nevertheless, which, as a local wit observed, is very much as if the American ,colonel of legendary fame had persisted in firing at the" gone coon" after he had come down. The worst part of the business is that in one instance at-least an experimental dynamite explosion is 'strongly suspected of having actually driven away a‘very promising gift of clouds.

'The gymnasts of Warrington and Bury met at Zury on Saturday evening, to decide which team should be entitled to enter the second round. The competition took place in the Athemeum, a very .commodious building, which was packed with spectators to witness the struggle. A large number of enthusiastic Warringtonians, including several members of the ladies', classes, had put in an ap- pearance, and taken.possession of the front seats. giving thaffarringtonians a hearty cheer as they marched on the stage at 7-30, the time arranged for the commencement of the contest. The items in the competition this year are—High jump,4 ft. 2 in one mark, and one mark for every inch over; clubs mass exercise, maximum ,marks 160; rings, maxi- mum l 0 each. This is thefirst year the Bury team bare entered the contest, so that they were almost an " .unknown quantity;' but as the teams faced each other on the stage, and the great superiority in physique of the Warrington men was noticed, expressions were freely passed that Warrington had a" soft thing" on, and so it proved. In the first item, jumping, Warrington scored 80 points against their opponents' 26. .Two of the Bury men failed to clear the height,.:4 ft.-21n. necessary to qualify them for cne mark, Collins and Hpreight being the only respectable jumpers, Collins clearing 4ft. Pin., and BO getting eight marks, and Spreight getting seven marks. The Warringtonians, taking the difficul- ties of the run into consideration, jumped splendidly. Warren, who was supposed to be suffering from a sprained knee, cleared sft4in. in fine style, J. Podmore coming next with 51t:1in. Mottram surprised every- one by clearing,sft. D. Walsh was rather below hi j s usual jump with .4ft. fin., G. Vernon 4ft. 10in., the brothers Hohnes 4ft..,9in. each, and T. Locker 4ft. ffin. When the judge,Mr.Renshaw,of the ManchekterY.M.C.A. Gymnasium, gave out the figuseg, Warrington leading by 54 points on the first item, it.seemsd to put quite a damper on the enthusiasm of the.audience, with the ex- ception of the Warrington section. The clubs came next, Bury first going through a Urge number of exer- cises in a very creditable manner; but, had they per- formed to music, they would have mated a much better impression. The judge recognized ,the merit of their performance by awarding:l2o marks. The Warrington- ians performed their exercises to waltanausic in splendid time, the whole audience applauding heartily at the finish, the judge awarding 130 marks. He remarked, at the same time, that he consided the various exercises performed by Bury quite as beneficial As those by War- rington, but that there were more mistakes made In their performance. That gave Warrington a lead of 64 points. The last item, the rings, Warrington, again as- serted their superiority, scoring 16 more points than their opponents, J. Podmore giving a fine .exhibition of how rings should be worked, and scoring 18 marks, while G. Vernon ran him close with 16, A. Whittle being the test man on the Bury side, scoring 16 marks. avyzabad llindoo has been restored Ito his caste by the following process of so-called "purification." The offence by which he lost caste was ebat of eat- ing cooked food in a railway carriage in which persons .of another caste were travelling. He had to pay his own weight first in pice, the amount reaching one hnndred and eighty rupees, and then in wheat. After being twice weighed in this way he was made to sit on a square stone, while his body was covered with cow dung,the face only excepted. He was then taken up by two men and thrown into the river, and after a good bath he came out and was received by the Brahmins, fully restored to caste-fellowship. The Brahmins informed the "purified" individual that a great favour had been conferred on him in weighing him in copper instead of silver

By LILLIAS WASSERMAN, Author of "Some Fisher Folk,* "Judith," "When the North .Wind Blows," c.

CLIAPTER, VIL A. TsuNnEnsmoit:itf: 'Before long the weather changed for the better, and under the softening influence of a great pleasant rushing west wind, accompanied by brilliant, though fitful sunshine, the snow dfifts melted away and vanished in a surprisingly rapid fashion. Lady Callerley, who had been impatiently awaiting this transformation scene, hailed its advent with rapturous delight. Now at last she would be able to oarzy out her

desire, and mount her bonny steea Briton;art. The pretty creature was growing to know and be exoeedingly fond of her young mistreis, to judge by the way in which its ears were priaked up at the sound of her voice, and the manner in which it followed her about, when she came into the stable yard where it was being groomed. Silvia's spirits rose to an effervescing point when she took her first ride, and Sir Lancelot praised her seat and gave her a few hints upon managing her
horse. The country assumed a new aspect when viewed under these circumstances, and the bride bid fair

to be completely reconciled to her surroundings. There was, however' one great drawback now to her contentment, and that was the continued pre- sence of her husband's cousin, Mrs. Breamish. That lady did not evince any great desire to return to her home and husband; and Silvia-chafed under her enforced companionship. Once or twice she ventured to pity the Squire, left to loneliness, in a significant fashion, but Dorothy Breamish would not take the hint. "Do not waste your sympathy, Silvia, my Child," she said sweetly, ignoring any further meaning in Lady C "so words, so long as the frost lasted, Harry Breamish might perhaps be a trifle moved, though even then there are 'his dogs and horses to be seen to and compared with others, his kennels and stables to set in order—but now that the thaw has come and he is able to hunt again there is no fear of his missing either Lance or me. You set too high a value on my society if you fancy my 'husband would pine in my absence." "I should not like to think that Lancelot would not miss me during so long a time," replied Lady Callerley, with sharpness. Madam laraghed lightly. " Ah, yes, of course. But you are young to matrimony, my dear, and still keep some of the sweet illusions we women prize BO highly. Besides, it is early days for-your husband to be tired of you yet, is it opt?" Silvia started, as if she were stung, but kept silence. She did not altogether understand. her husband, and there was very small indication of any lover- like fervour about him. Therefore did Madam's words irritate and wound her, as they probalily were meant to do, since the speaker watched their effect with a close and cat-like scrutiny. They also had the effect of stopping any furtlier attempts on Silvia's part to get rid of her unwel- come guest. Lady Callerley sighed, but submitted to the infliction with a bad grace. Without being absolutely inhospitable she could not say more than she had done already. And Sir Lancelot so evidently enjoyed his conein't society that even the inexperienced and impalsivt wife recognised that she must not dare to appeal rude, As Silvia failed to fathom many of het husband's moods, she grew more, rather than less, afraid of him- There at times were-dark fits which fell overlisspirit ; times when his reserve deepened and bin temper grew uncertain; and at such taxies it was neither pleasant nor safe to cross him. The girl was too young and ignorant to under- stand wherein her relations with him failed but she was not too young and ignorant to feel, with a keen semse of disappointment, that they &A so. She longed, with all the enthusiastic fervour-of an affectionate nature, to love him entirely, to under- stand him thoroughly, to be one with him in heart, and soul, and body. But some subtle, indefinite, and yet perfectly impassable barrier lay between, ever repelling and shutting out with (Sold, hard, immutability, the delicate, sensitive appeals given by the awakening heart of the bride, appeals asking in vain for the perfected sympathy of a true mar- riage. One brilliant and yet changeful 'day in earV spring, Lady Callerley was tempted to stroll further than usual, and found herself on the far side of the burn at the bottom of the Avenue before she recognised that she was a long way from home, and unaccompanied. Sir Lancelot, riding some distance that afternoon, had decided that Silvia must not. go with him. She had a restless fit upon her, and after his departure found it impossible to remain indoors. Besides, a long afternoon with Mrs. Brearaish, whom she distrusted more and more every day, and whose caressing manner and smooth speech made her feel rebellious, was not to be endured. The caressing manner was neither nature/ nor true, and the smooth speech, when analysed, was apt to contain little stinging darts. Perhaps some smart left by the said darts now rOBO in Silvia's memory as she stood hesitating, and influenced her finally against returning; for she took instead the path leading down to the sea. Before long, however, she had reason to regret her decision, and the great distance she was from any shelter. The treacherous sun shining so brightly when she first set out, withdrew suddenly behind a veil a mist, and with terrible rapidity thunder clouds rolled up from the horizon. Lady Callerley began to feel slightly ntlFvous as the sky blackened and dropped down upon the sea, as though it would fain blot out that great waste of sull,en, throbbing' water, lying so dark beneath it. What a desolate, wild, savage sort of place this North-country was, the little town-bred creature thought, with a shudder, as she looked first at the grey sea, with nothing to break its monotony but the white crests of foam leaping to life upon every tossing wave, and then at the long dreary stretches of sandhills, likewise unbroken,v, save by the cliff upon which stood the ruined church of Callerley with its clustering gravestones, and the little head- land to the south that sheltered Breamish Harbour sandhills of monotonous colour and outline that form the coastline for a few miles at either side of Yarrop Burn. Beyond the village of Breamish the character of the coast changed to advantage, so far as pie- tureaqueness was concerned, becoming rugged and rocky sandstone cliffs of considerable height, pierced and undermined by the action of the sea, forming a convenient refuge for the free-traders, alternating with pretty sheltered bays, which had often little fishing villages nestling close down to them, and fleets of boats an'ehored within their harbours. But that was further than Lady Callerley could see.
The barrenness and the lonelhess of the near prospect frightened her. There seemed ,no living creature but herself in,this big, dead, awe-inspiring world.

• She started in .alarm when a wide-winged sea- gull swooped down, close overhead, in one of its gra:eeful circling flights, and its sad, harsh, plain- tive cry broke sucldenky upon the stillness. But a moment afterwards she followed the ex- sznple of the ancient mariner, and blessed it un- awares. It lifted the weight :from her heart, the weight of solitude that was pressing there so heavily; she felt glad of its presence since it alko had the gift of life. lier wistful ewes followed ..the beautiful strong- winged creature, as it drew away in ever widening circles from the land. For one moment its wings showed up, an intense white, against the inky background of cloud; the next, It was lost to sight behind that same background. Lady Callerley turned home Wards, but as she did so a sudden flash of fire darted down from the black sky to the black sea, lighting up all the miles and miles of heaving billows with instantaneous and lurid illumination, leaving them when it was Over darker thnti before. Swift upon this followed the battle roll of the thunder, breaking immediately overhead in oue tremendous crash, and then gradually dying out in sullen reverberations along the barren shore. Then a great drop of rain fell upon Silvia's up. turned face, and she looked despairingly around fat sb.lter. ' ehe pieced a fittlai:ltooking wooden brings, under wh.ft‘ the brawling.burn ran to join the sea, , ,thifa eke her hope a house must be near. Sure enough a cottage came in sight perched upon a sarulhill near to the mouth of the burn. A cottage belonging to filtherfolk evidently. Nets of a ruddy colour were draped about the palings. of the gardens, strings of bladders festooned the wu thoh dooorvraeyna. a boe rothwr rt n articles liewles was a proppedhing g er lay u pf against about the front of the house. Whatever it was there was shelter to be obtained within four wall, and tmder a roof, ant Lady Qacrivy made for it
CHAPTER VIII.

A FISHER LASS. When the little lady flew up, panting and breath- less, she became aware that just within the door of the cottage leaned a girl, a girl whose profile showed fair against the dark interior. Lady Callerley gasped out a hasty request for shelter until the storm should be over, and the girl, who was engaged in mending a net, smiled and nodded assent at once. The visitor entered and waited, and after a minute or two, the fisher girl brought forward a chair and placed it close by the fire, still, however, without making any remark or speaking a word of welcome. It was the first cottage Silvia had visited since she came to Seaton Callerley, and she looked around with curiosity and interest. There was not then any education in art for the generality of the people, and for lack, perhaps, of education what is , now designated the picturesque, was then only , knowns the slovenly and the common; wherefore it did iTot strike Silvia that brown sails lying heaped up in a corner, tanned nets, creels and baskets, tangles of ribbon weed hung against the wall to act as barometers—they being dry and crackly in fine and limp and flabby in stormy weather—helped to form an interior in which a painter would have seen a picture ready composed to his hand. Even the battered relics of ships long gone down to ,the deep that were to be seen here and there scattered about the place, helped to add to the character and completeness of a fisher dwelling. One thing, however, did impress Lady Callerley favourably, and that was the exceedingly great beauty of the girl who had admitted her. Never h.t.a she come 'across such a splendid specimen of rustic womanhood before. What ass more astonishing than all else about the fisher lass, was the extreme composure and dignity of manner she possessed. Not all the train- ing of a Court beauty could have given to her more of this than nature had implanted already. Although she had uttered no spoken welcome to Lady Callerley, the latter saw in a moment that this was from no rude or ungracious mood. She ' did not require the explanatory glance towards the place where the figure of an old woman, apparently slumbering, sat in an arm-chair, in the single nook, to Ailialre her of this point. The girl returned to her work, leaning against the side of the door, in seeming indifference both to the unaccustomed visitor and to the storm now raging with such violence outside. Though so untrained in art, Lady Callerley had yet seen some of the most famous statues of the world during the tour she had made abroad with Lady Ormskirk the previous year, and she was re- minded both of the Venus de Milo and of the Clytie, as she looked at this beautiful fisher girL There was the same fine arch of brow, with the rippling yellow hair growing low upon it, and the exquisite curve of neck down drooping, as in the Clytie ; while the grand majestic outlines of figure and limbs, and a certain calm dignity of bearing, were certainly the attributes of the famous Venus. For the rest, the clear grey eyes, large, well-formed mouth, and rich sunburnt complexion, glowing with youth and perfect health, were the special gifts of the race to which she belonged ; characteristic of the Norse blood, transmitted from bygone genera- tions of sea robbers and invaders.

The girl was dressed pretty much in the same style as our fisher lasses favour now, that is to say, in a print bodice, and a skirt of coarse blue flannel. The waist was a little shorter, and the skirt a trifle longer, though, happily, not long enough to hide the bare and well-shaped brown feet and ankles.

As the storm darkened in aiore and more, the girl could no longer see to do her work, and drew nearer to the fire, and just then a terrible peal of thunder shook the cottage, and awakened the old woman, who rubbed her eyes and looked astonished at Silvia's presence. " Darreay it's a wild sort o' day, Bell? Eigh weigh ! A windy March, and a showery April, make a bonnie May. An' whatten a little lady's this ye've gettin' ti bear ye company, while yer awd granny took her nap? Aa'm thinkin' ye'll be fra' Breamish Hall, or a lassie belangin' to some o' th' new Lady Callerley's friends maybe?" Silvia was used to being taken for an extremely young girl, so she only laughed. "I'm Lady Ca'allerlay herself, though I fancy you will find it difficult to credit it." With great trouble the old woman got off her seat when she heard this statement, and made a low tremulous curtsey. "Aw served the Callerleys mony and mony a laag year," she said, in a quivering voice, "an' it's a great honour to see th' New Leddy under ma poor roof. Aw norsed yer goodman, and his father afore him ; but noo aw'rn aad and useless, and its lang or aa;ve seen ony o' th' breed. Though it's none so wonderful that he shouldn't care to live in a place where they all died.afore their times." "Granny," broke in the clear strong voice of Bell, "ye manna frighten th' leddy to start wi'; she's nigh on a hunnerd, poor aad body, an' whiles her mind wanders sore, so ye must just excuse her;" she went on to .Silvia in apology. "Nigh on a hunnerd? A hunnerd last June ye mean, ye hussy!" said the old woman, angrily, as terribly afraid of being cheated out of a year of her abnormally long life as she might have been of having one added to it sixty years before. "It's a great age, and aa'vp seen a lot o' life, ma dear! So when ye want to learn anythin' about what's hap- pened on th' estate, ye've only got to come to me; for ma memory's fair wonderful, spite o' what yon lass says, and aw could tell ye things that would interest ye, noo ye're a Callerley! But hoo cam Sir Lancelot te pass ewer Madam, and fall in love wi' a bit lam like ye, aw wonder ?—not that ye're no canny and bonnie too, wi' yer blue eyes and yer innocent like face, but to bear th' wight o' an awd name, and te help him te banish fra his mind what the future hes i' store for him." "Whist thee now, granny, an' divvint weary Leddy Callerley wi' yor fond clash," again en- treated Bell. It seemed to Silvia that the girl was quite nervous lest the old woman might chance to say sornethins which she herself was not to hear. Lady Callerley was half attracted, and half re- pelled by the strange old creature. No one could have conic nearer to her conception of a witch, and there was a weird feeling produced in her by the queer, incomprehensible mutterings from the chimney corner. These utterances were not easy to follow; partly from the fact that to a Southern ear, the Northum- brian dialect is all but unintelligible, sounding like some guttural foreign tongue with its burr and its sing-song, and also because the loss of teeth made them exceedingly indistinct. Nevertheless Lady Callerley gathered sufficient from them to induce her to long with piqued and surprised curiosity for further revelatioas. Nanny Widdiington, the sybil of the district, was a typical Northumbrian of the old school, one of a sort now fast becoming obsolete. Superstitions to an incredible degree ; ever on the look out for omens of bad or good fortune; an in- terpreter of dreams and visions; full of quaint, blood-curdling stories, concerning bogies, witches, and ghosts ; with strong belief in the efficacy of horseshoes to bring lack, and the branches of moun- tain ash or Whicken-tree, as it is called, to guard the possessor and ward off danger. In this she was not singular either; for in her young days there was such a mist of fear and credulity over this country, that men trembled at every sound heard after nightfall, lei it might be something uncanny, and made use of all sorts of spells and antidotes against the malignant influences by which they fancied themselves surrounded. The bolts of doors must be cut from the rowan tree wood, that evil things might not cross the threshold, and even sailors must carry a berried twig of this wonderful " witch- wood " aboard their ships, that they might be safe from the powers of the air, and have favouring winds on their vevagest. in person, IN anny Woken not at all until° a witch -rself, as Lady Callerley thotight, with her face resembling a withered walnut, minus the shell, and bright, beady eyes winking out from it; nose and ,chin all but meeting, and head swathed,in a red cotton handkerchief. She was so very old, death seemed to have passed her by. She had outlived two generations, and now was left to the care of her great grandchildren. A relic of the past truly! They were very kind to her, especially the girl Bell, and she enjoyed life in her own fashion, and was not at all anxious to be rid of it, especially now that she had outlived even her chronic rheumatism. She liked to see the young ones shiver and grow cold, as she prophesied ilnuck, or told them her dreams, which were alio strangely prophetic, generally prophetic of evil The storm was passing over and Bell began to bustle about and prepare for the Mime-corning of the lads, her brothers, who were down at Breamish, busy with their boats, and who would be in presently, both cold and hungry. Silvia watched her with an almost childish pleasure at the sight ot anything so perfectly natural and gracefuL The easy, harmonious move- twos,. instinct with quiet strength, and the beauty

The ear, too, was filled and satisfied with the clear, pure, full voice that came and went in snatches of ballads, as Bell moved about the place. These snatches sounded strange, and not quite proper to; the town-bred lady, but were evidently innocent of all wrong meaning to the singer. "If yor goodman be crabbed au' gray, Mebbe yell oft be sad ; Yet nivvor wear yor heart away, On any sailor lad ! "For gin ye lie awake o' nights, An' hear the storm blaw free ; Ye'll wish the yen was safe ashore, The t'other in the sea !" Lady Callerley was charmed with the cottage and its inmates, and mentally decided that it not be long before she found her way thilber again. In the meantime, she began to wonder how she should get home again. The heavy clouds were gone, and a line of yellow sky lay over the sea. But the grass of the souLl" would hills would be wet and slippery, and should she unfortunate enough to take cold, it would be fare" well to solitary rambles from henceforth. But Bell's quick eyes discerned a rescue in tbo

distance. " Yonder's Sir Lancelot on his black horse, Ina. leddy 1" she said, suddenly, pausing by the oPen, door. "Must aw give him a wave o' the hwicleas let him know ye're here Oh, yes! there, sure enough, was her husbaalha riding by on his horse Despair, and very gine surprised to see his wife abroad in such weatheras But the rain was over, and the thunder clouds ha rolled away, and with a promise to come sifal/I' soon, Silvia left the cottage. "Take me up, Lancelot !" she cried, and Ir.ln she set her little foot on his, stooping, he her behind behind him, and they rode home in a comal manner of the day, when all farmer's vvives daughters, and most of the squires, too, for "a- matter, were contented to ride pillion. "So you have been to see my old nurse' deed:, remarked Sir Lancelot, kindly; but to mind he did not seem quite to approve of we visit. He felt sure that Nanny would chattuer about family affairs, and wanted to know what a"„e„, had said. But Silvia was rapidly learning to leer noel*. her own counsel, and made him an evasive a In her mind she was now conscious of a mrtell' evidently meant to be hidden from her by everyone; but safe to crop out sooner or later. She meant tia return to the cottage, and if poirsible see the woman alone. There would not be much diffiein" in getting Nanny to talk if Bell were not there guard her utterances. It was too had of the little creature to 14 curious, but she was a true daughter of Eve ; besides, she hated to be treated like a child. the heart swelled with anger and injustice at, thought that Lancelot did not trust her. F 13,," not kept all Teddy's secrets most carefully? sure Teddy's secrets were gel:A:a-ally the talk d " i t—c, town, and after telling no end of white lies 90 guard them, it was provoking to find everyone r well acquainted with them as herself. 14e,..vve mind! She could keep them, and that was thing.

div.p: 'IMPRESSIVE SCENES.

The funeral of the late Duke of Clarence took Cane at Sandringham on Wednesday. The morning Sandringham was cold but fine, and soon after IlaYlight visitors began to flock into the place from tile surrounding villages. At half-past nine o'clock ' 'the escort proceeded from Dersingh am to the church, llnd drew up outside the lycbgate. There also were theikamekeepers and labourers on the estate, who 'cl'ere formed up in column and afterwards followed 113ntittha hwe r procession. The school children stood on the leading from the lycbgate to the park Sates, while outside were gathered little groups of Venple who had come to pay a last tribnte of re- Vect to the memory of the late Duke. At a quarter ten o'clock the escort was moved away a little tance from the church to wait until the condo- ton of the service. The gun-carriage was drawn • 3' Six horses. The pathway leading from the park gates to the highroad was kept by a small force of iTnnty police, but their duty was purely formal, Lars being no unseemly crowding on the part of ne spectators. The passing bell in the belfry of &Jae church then began to toll. At a quarter past •„ten o'clock three carriages drove round from the ''inse to the church. In the first was the Prince of Wales, and in the second the Princess of Wales and the young Princesses. Having entered the Church, a brief sermon was performed, and at its conclusion the procession proceeded to Wolferton atation, large crowds lining the route. AT WINDSOR. • . The Great Keep of Windsor Castle has looked down on Inany histbric scenes, the pride and pomp of kings, the Q4dttings and goings of Ministries, and other moving 4ncidents connected with Crown and State ; but never Ilave its grey walls witnessed a scene at once so tender • kid dramatic as that which was enacted, when, in the Presence of his bride, the mortal remains of the Duke of 411arence were lowered into their last resting-place under we very altar where a month hence his Royal Highness to have stood as a bridegroom. It seemed to touch trroheart of everyone, and as the body was borne ' ugh the mournful streets one deep sob burst from fronts Lla of lips. Every shop was closed, and on the !nest of them were hung black and white • an '"Ves, which served to hide the somewhat mean learance of the Windsor streets. 320 t three o'clock a signal from the Round Tower an- be , .11Peed the arrival of the Royal train, a few minutes ••Ind time. The Duke of Edinburgh, the Duke of Con- . tight, Prince Henry of Battenberg, Prince Christian, *tle Marquis of Lorne, the Duke of Teck, and other mem- ' •be ‘rs of the Royal Family were awaiting it. One of the u‘tendants carried a wreath newly arrived from Osborne, . . . .
