The Master cf the Horse. Followed by The Gentlemen in Attendance on the Royal personages. Adjutant General. Quarter Master General. Escort of the 2nd Life Guards. rho procession moved along the road under the Castle walls to the music of the Dead March in "Saul," played by the massed bands, and this was presently changed to the equally mournful music of Chopin's Funeral March, accompanied by the heavy roll of muffled drums. Minute guns were now fired by a battery of artillery stationed in the Long Walk. The head of the cortege having reached the entrance of the chapel, the music of Chopin's march came to a dead stop, the bands fell out of line, and the mourners passed out of sight. It was now close upon four o'clock and getting dusk, and a biting wind swept the Castle grounds. Nevertheless the crowds lingered long about the scene of this deeply impressive ceremonial. WITHIN T. GEORGE'S CHAPEL. The doors were opened soon after two o'clock, and very quickly the nave was filled. There marched in at the south door Sir F. Leighton,P.R.A., Lord Arthur Hilt, Lord Spencer, Lord Wolseley, Mr.Stanhope,Lord George Hamilton Mr. Chaplin and Lord Colvillo of Culross. Immediate ' Immediately afterwards Prince Christian went down the central aisle and took his place at the west door to be ready to join the funeral ptocession. Probably his im- paired sight made him unwilling to risk the walk through the streets. It was now thrce o'clock, the time when the service ought to have begun,and those inside the chapel listened anxiously for the sound of the minute-guns in the Long Walk. The organist meanwhile played various soft and wailing pieces of music. The red curtains over the door were now drawn aside, and Lord Lathom advanced to take charge of the procession. It advanced up the aisle in the following order : Servants of his late Royal Highness. The Equerries to his late Royal Highness. Bearing the Insignia of his late Royal Highness. The Comptroller and Treasurer of his late Royal High- ness, bearing the Coronet of his late Royal Highness. The Choir. The Canons of Windsor. The Rev. Frederick Hervey. Domestic Chaplain to His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales. The Very Rev. the Dean of The Bishop of Rochester, Windsor. Clerk of the Closet to Her Majesty. The Comptroller, Lerd Chamberlain's Department. The Vice Chamber- The Comptroller The Tieasurer of of the House- the Household. hold. The Lord Steward. The Lord Chamberlain. Supporters of the Supporters of the Pall, Pall, Officers of the Officers of the 10th Royal THE COFFIN, 10th Royal Hussars (Prince Hussars (Prince of Wales's Own). of Wales's Own). Borne by men of the 10th Royal Hussars. Garter King-of-Arms. The Chief Mourner, HIS ROYAL HIGHNESS THE PRINCE OF WALES, K.G. , supported by his Royal Highness Prince George of Wales, KG., and the Duke of Fife K.T., followed by the Royal Family and Royal persenages, as before arranged, and the attendants upon their Royal Highnesses. The choir preceded the coffin. They sang very beauti- fully the opening sentences of the most impressive burial service of the Church of England. The coffin itself, carried by soldiers of the 10th HuAars., and with the pall supported by officers of the regiment, was most tastefully decorated. Often in modern times such pro- cessions have been spoiled by a too lavish display of flowers, which have presented an indiscriminate mass too large "and too similar in its parts for beauty. But the late Duke of Clarence's coffin was ornamented with an economy of material which appealed to one's sense of good taste. At the front part af the coffin, ccvered with the Union Jack, were two wreaths—one a floral cross and the other in the form of a harp with some of its strings broken. The latter was from the Princess Vic- toria Mary, who perhaps had been thinking of Lord Tennyson's lines, though written Is, another connection, about the " rift within the lover's lute" which bad "made the music mute." Behind these two wreaths was placed the late Prince's Hussar busby with its white plume, and the rest of the coffin was simply covered with lilies of the valley. The Prince of Wales, with his son Prince George of Wales, walked immediately behind the coffin. The Prince's head was bowed down, and he was obviously feeling intense grief; and even still more complete physical exhaustion. With many Royal per- sons and representations of other Royal persons follow- ing behind, the procession passed into the choir. The Princess of Wales, her daughters, and the Princess Vic- toria Mary were in the chapel, but they had entered by a private way, were secluded ilia dark g allery, and few if any, saw them. At the close of the service the Bishop pronounced the solemn Benediction. Then the Prince of Wales advanced and placed a little cross of white flowers on the coffin, and then with slow and reverent steps he, followed by other members of the Royal Family and princely representatives of foreige monarchs, passed in single file from St. George's Chapel, leaving the dead prince in company only with the emblems of departed greatness.

SERVICE AT OSBORNE. The "Court Circular" of Wednesday evening states that the Queen and Princess Louise and the members of the Royal Household attended a special service in the chapel at Osborne on Wednesday afternoon in memory of His Royal Highness the Duke of Clarence and Avon- dale. The Rev. Canon Duckworth officiated. The memorial service consisted of sentences from the Burial Service, the 4mn "Let saints on earth," the lesson of selected passages, the collect for Easter-eve, the hymn " 0, let him whose sorrow," prayer from the Burial Service, a special prayer, the hymn "The saints of God," and the Benediction. Funeral marches by Chopin and Beethoven were played by the band of the King's Royal Rifles before and after the service. Minute guns were fired from Her Majesty's ship Invincible during the service.

div.head: LONDON IN MOURNING.
div.p: LONDON IN MOURNING.

It is many years since any public event has made itself so, evident in the streets of London as the funeral of the late Duke of Clarence. Everywhere the number of people dressed in black was noticeable, blinds were drawn down at all the public buildings and in many private houses, there were shutters before the windows of the great majority of shops, and flags on almost every flagpost at half-mast, even to the little "Jacks "which decorate certain omnibuses. The Stock Exchange did not open, and some shops were closed thdotwhole day ; but it was not until noon that the demonstration became most remarkable. The scene in the city after midday was more striking. Shops and warehouses were closed, and by a common impulse all the streams of traffic which struggled unceasingly in Cheapside, Fleet-street, and other City thoroughfares seemed turned in one direction. The employ-es steamed in hundreds from the great places of business in their working clothes and mingled with the crowds of mourners who came in cabs, omnibuses, and on foot from all points of the compass and thronged the streets leading to St. Paul's. By one o'clock the great area of St. Paul's Churchyard was filled by a mor or less motley crowd, which increased every momente At three o'clock the Lord Mayor and Sheriffs arrived in State coaches, the brilliant colours of the vehicles and the liveries showing even more resplendent than usual against the sombre backgrdusd. A way was made. The great west door was thrown open, and in decorous silence the civic dignitaries entered. Many of the crowd then left; but many thousands remained outside during the whole service, those favourably placed catching occasional glimpses of the interior as the door opened and fainting or hysterical women were carried out. With the conclusion of the service the crowd slowly dis- persed. At four o'clock some of the business establish- ments reopened, but the gloom of the day still pervaded the wholecity. Almost every theatre and place of entertafiiinent was dosed' at night, and neither nieetings nor social festivities were held. Throughout the country, and in the chief cities of the Continent„ as well as of India and the British Colonies solemn memorial services were held.

div.head: .WARRINGTON.
div.p: .WARRINGTON.

On Thursday the day of the funerat9f the late Dike of Clarence, a few shops were closed in Warrington dur- ing the morning, and a number of others were closed, in accordance with the Mayor's published request. from two to four o'clock in the afternoon. Flags were exhi- bited half mast high at the Town Hall, St. James's Church, and other places, and a muffled knell was rung on the curfew bell at Holy Trinity Church during the afternoon. A special memorial service was held during the same part of the day, at which there was a very large congregation, including the Mayor (Alder- man Greenall) and Aldermen Francomb, Wright, and Burgess. The service for the burial of the dead was first read by the Sector(the Rev. F. W. Willis),and after- wards the "Dead March" was played by the organist, Mr. W. 8. Woods. The lessons were read by the Rev. C.-E. Jackson, and assistance was given in the service by the Revs. F. C. Timmis and T. E. Cook. The service was concluded by, the rendering of Chopin's funeral march on the organ.

STORIES ABOUT THE LATE DUKE. A MALL LOVE ROMANCE. The Duke (says" Land And Water ") was a lover so loyal that he has made a story of a Royal and honourable love read almost like .a romance. And here it was that his Strength of character was shown. He loved his con- sin May. For reasons about which it would be imper- tinent for a subject to conjecture, this boy's and girl's, this children's affection—for it began very early—was always discountenanced. Prince Edward was always obedient ; but his negative opposition could not be suis- dued. The marriageable Protestant Royalty in Europe was passed in review before him. Alliance after alliance was suggested. Nothing caused him to swerve in his loyalty to his cousin. Time flew by ; the age at which Orince in this line of direct succession should marry was attained and left behind, and those very State rea-

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JA
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JA

sons which stood against them were at last found, in the flight of days, standing commandingly on his side. His betrothal to the Princess Mary was a peaceful, but very honourable, triumph of love and virtue. Would that vic- tory had come earlier ! A GIPSY'S WARNING.

Several years ago (says the" ") it was stated by one well acquainted with the inner life of Marlborough House. that the reason why Prince Albert Victor showed no disposition to marry was that he had been " fright- ened' ' by the prediction of a gipsy, who, knowing no- thing of his rank, had once told him his fortune. The woman's prediction was to the effect that marriage would mean death to him. It was said that on trying his luck a second time with another fortune teller he had received a similar warning against contemplating matri- mony. The story would not be worth telling now, but for the fact that it was undoubtedly current in London society some years ago.

THE DEER AND MR. GLADSTONE. " I was only once," writes a correspondent in the "Speaker," close to the Duke of Clarencp for a number of hours at a stretch. It was on the memorable after- noon in the spring of 1386 when Mr. Gladstone brought in his Home Rule Bill for Ireland. It was my good fortune to have a seat in the Ambassadors' Gallery on that occasion, and T found myself sitting just beilind the Prince of Wales and his elder son. Both listened, as all the crowded house did, with breathless attention to the three hours' harangue in which the great orator unfolded his proposals for a new and better way for Ireland. When he sat down, exhausted by an effort which might well have tried a younger man, there was a loud outburst of cheering from the members of every party. To my surprise I heard the sounds of applause close to me in the gallery—an unprecedented breach of rules. I looked up and saws' prince Eddie " vigorously clapping his hands. Far be it from me to suggest that he had any sympathy with Mr, Gladstone's policy. He may or may not have had such sympathy, but of that I know nothing. What was evident was that the generosity of youth had drawn from him a spontaneous tribute to the genius and eloquence of a great veteran. I own I admired him for the frankness and naiveté of his display of feeling."

interest, too; and all who had come to the service that morning expected, no doubt, that some prominent men- tion would be made of the great sorrow which had fallen on the nation. All hearts had been moved to deepest sympathy with the Royal household in the great loss they had sdstained. The Methodists had always been a loyal people. Humble addresses of congratulation or condolence had been forwarded to her Majesty again and again by the Conference, in the name of the Methodist people, onAhe occasion of the joys or sorrows that had coma to her and the Royal family during her long reign. And In this great loss, the loss of the heir presumptive to the throne, they would not be behind other churches in the expression of their sympathy. The preacher having given a briet sketch of the late Duke's career, pro- ceeded to say that he was engaged to he married to the Princess Mary of Teck. The news gave great satisfac- tion. Et was believed to be a connection brought about by pure affection, and not by ministers for reasons of I State. The day of the marriage wee fixed, preparations had reached an advanced Stage, the fulness of life was opening before the Duke, a few days of illness came, the result of a cold taken at a funeral, and all was over. It was a domestic tragedy by which all hearts were touched into grief. The preacher than mentioned some of the characteristics of the Prince including sweetness of temper, reserve, kindness and consideration for others, ' and devotion to his parents. The. impressive sermon was brought to a close by the playing of the Dead March in "Saul," which was rendered with great feeling by the chapel organist, Mr. James Muir. The pulpit at Bold-street Chapel was occupied in the evening by the rev, gentleman, who again referredto the death of the Duke.

ST. ALBAN'S, BEWSET-STREET. A memorial service was held in this church on Sunday morning, with reference to the late Cardinal. The high altar was draped in black, and during the mass the choir sang portions of the well-known Requiem. After the gospel, the Rev. Father Feeney, ascended the altar steps, and preached a panegyric on Cardinal Manning, at the same time contrasting the two deaths, that of the Royal. Prince, taken away in the very midst of life, and the Prince of the Church bowed down with the weight of years, and a life full of merit and noble toil. The reverend preacher took for his text 1 Corinthians, ix., 19 and 22—" For whereas I was free as to all, I made myself the servant of all," Btc. The sermon was an exposition of this text. At the close of the service, the Dead March in "Saul" was played on the organ, the whole congregation remaining in the church till its conclusion. , COCKHEDOE MISSION. At this mission on Sunday evening, the Rev. John Davies referred to the mournful occurrence of last week the death of the Duke of Clarence. Instead of the wed- ding carriages, and the joyous ginists,and the happiness which would have reigned throughout, they would now have the solemn funeral procession,and mourning would reign instead of joy. The sympathy of the whole nation would go forth to the parents and relatives and his affianced bride, who had all her hopes dashed to the ground. .

7 CAIRO-STREET CHAPEL. At Cairo-street Chapel, on Sunday evening, the Rev. Frank K. Freeston took for his text: "Thus saith the Lord, Set thy house in order, for thou shalt die and not live." (11. Kings, xx. 1.) He said that during the previous week the edict of death had summoned from earth many well-known men in their various spheres, including two bishops, two peers who were friends of the people, two professors of science. and two members of Parliament, of whom one represented the neighbour- ing town of Liverpool. But there stood out first on this long obituary list two other names in particular, one because of his age and noble reputation, the other because of his youth and royal position. To these two names he wished to refer. On Thursday morning had died Cardinal Manning. They had lost at last" the poor man's Cardinal," but only after a long and labori- ous life devoted to the service of his fellow men. He was a Catholic and they were not, and he had often been treated with Protestant prejudice. But good deeds knew no distinction of faith, and Englishmen came to look at length, not at the red hat of the Cardinal, but at the warm heart of the man. No official religious leader of our time had pet his religion to more practical purpose in all questions affecting the real welfare of the working-classes. They would aU remember his efforts is a member of the Royal Commission on the Housing of the Poor, and not be likely to forget the important part he took iii the great dockers' strike in London in 1889, and the complete confidence placed in him by both sides in the dispute. No question affecting the condition of the people, their homes, their temptations, tbe cruelty practised upon their children, was left without his wise and large-hearted consideration ; and of all these social questions he placed the most stress on temperance, which to him meant total abstinence. By the death of Cardinal Manning the Catholic Church had lost a leader whom they would find it very difficult to replace, the nineteenth century had lost a • unique. figure whose _ memory history would, however, gratefully preserve, and every labourer for right, of whatever church or faith, had lost a champion and a counsellor whose deeds and whose words were a tower of strength, and who loved his fellow-men. But he had set his house in order, and 'Was calmly ready to die. A few minutes after the aged Cardinal had passed to his rest he was followed by the royal youth whose years were but a third his number. If there was anyone in the world who could be pointed Out as fortune's first favourite, it was the eldest son of the Heir-apparent to the throne of mighty England. 'Born into the highest lot which outward circumstances could confer, destined, as it seemed, to be England's future king, recently betrothed to one whom many loved, with congratulations showered upon him and marriage festivities all awaiting him, he was the central figure of court liN and the almost hourly subject of talk. Was not the brightest possible future about to bow down before him ? But almost ere England could realize that he was ill, the hand of death was laid upon him, this brilliant suture was wrenched from his grasp, and he had to lie down and die like the humblest amongst us, and enter an inheritance, not of this world. It was indeed a truly pathetic tragedy and he (the preacher), could not wonder that it had so deeply moved the coun- try. He deplored the outward parade of grief, and the conventional mourning and the idle warning about the danger to the monarchy and the altered course of history. At such a time he could forget the grades avid ranks of society and all the trappings of royalty, and think only of the stricken home, and of one who was to have been nearer and dearer than even father or mother or sisters or brother, and made a new home for them both. Death brought all humanity together, court and cottage, prince and peasant, royalty and poverty, monarchy and democracy. They were all one before God, who was no respecter of persons. Man proposes but God disposes, and the plain lesson of this most sudden and touching death was that each and all, both high and low, must set their house in order ere the days of strength had passed, and than be ready for God's call, whenever it should come. I ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH.

At St. John's Presbyterian Church, Winwick-st., on Sunday evening, the Rev. J. Warnock, who preached, he said: What may be the lesson which the Almighty means to teach by the sudden removal of the young Prince, for whom the nation now mourns, no one can say. The fact is plain enough, but who will give the

div.head: REFERENCES TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS
div.p: REFERENCES TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS
DEAD. WARRINGTON PULPIT REFRENCES. WYCLIFFE CHURCH.

- - Preaching to'a large congregation,at Wycliffe Church, on Sunday evening, the Rev. John Yonge made special reference to the death of the Duke of Clarence, and also I to that of Cardinal Manning. In the course of his re- ' marks, Mr. Yonge said that the first fortnight of the New Year had been heavily marked with inauspicious events. The death of Cardinal Manning could only be regarded as a great national loss, for he was an English- I man of lofty principle and noble character, and wide in- I fleence for good, however much, from their point of I I view, his religious and ecclesiastical career might give I occasion for regret. That he served God and his fellow- men with unswerving loyalty and devotion was aisun- dantly proved by his whole career. A very different I man, indeed, from the great Earl of Shaftesbury—the two being both theologically and ecclesiastically the poles asunder—yet Cardinal Manning seemed to have stepped into the philanthropic breach- caused by the death of that Famous nobleman, and he would be long remembered in this country more as the friend of the poor and oppressed, and as the champion of purity and temperance,than as,what undoubtedly he had also been, one of the greatest prince-prelates the Roman Church of .modern days had known. The great Cardinal died on the Thursday morning previous, and had not busy death been hotly bent on proving his power upon all ages, and all ranks alike probably the papers of the week and the pulpits of that day, had been largely taken up with the study of so remarkable and instructive a life. But on that same morning death achieved a yet more masterly stroke, by which he had drawn the saddened atten- tion and sympathy of the whole Empire and indeed of the whole civipsed world, around the home of the heir to the throne. Smiting down the aged Cardinal in his 84th year at half-past eight, the great leveller struck down the young Prince of 28 but an hour later. The second event had almost put the first out of sight. That was a fact which was very remarkable, Regarded as actual losses to the great human world; regarded in the com- parative value of their life record • the death of the Cardinal was much more, might they say, regrettable than that of the Prince. The Church of Christ and the human race had sustained in Dr. Manning's death, how- ever natural and inevitable at his age, a greater actual loss than in the death of the young Prince, whom, all the same, and with unaffected sincerity and sorrow, the whole country paused in its manifold activities and industries, and competitions and enterprises, to lament. It was unquestionable that never, since the death of the Prince Consort, in 1861, had the country been so univer- sally moved by any stroke of death as it was that day, by the sudden and unlooked for death of the Duke of Clarence. That profound emotion could not have been stirred by any personal attachment that the Duke had succeeded in drawing to himself from the nation at large. Except in name,the Prince had been almost, and largely of necessity, a stranger to the general com- munity. He had pursued a quiet unostentatious career through boyhood and youth up to manhood, and only very rarely had taken a personal part in national events. It was the youth and the position, and what were the immediately prospective circumstances of the dead Prince, which had called out that wide national sorrow. No more irresistibly pathetic event had occured in their time. Not even the death of the Queen's Consort, sad and desolating to the monarch and her family, much to be mourned also by the nation, as was that event, entirely paralleled that occurrence. The young Prince, just enter( d amid popular approval, upon the enjoyment of betrothal to a noble and beautiful girl, to whom, it was said, that for several. years he had been tenderly attached, looking forward in the course of a few brief weeks to what might have been one of the happiest of marriages; the day of the wedding actually fixed; the guests invited; the ceremonial in course of elaborate arrangement ; addresses of congratulation being prepared, in many cases accompanied by costly and magnificent presents, from all parts at the empire and of • the world; the young Prince in this his hour of hope and joy, was seized by illness which at• first indeed seemed almost trivial, and which he endeavoured to throw off as unworthy of serious account. Then his birthday in- tervened, and its festive celebration was naturally devised to be more joyous in anticipation of the new happiness which his new year seemed to hold out to him. But, alas, a 'shadow was on the birthday celebration. And when the dreaded news travelled far and wide few were the homes and callous indeed the hearts which for- bore that " fellow feeling which makes us all akin." SERMON BY THE REV. J. GUNNELL.

The morning service at Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapel was conducted by the Rev. John Gunnell," superintendent of the circuit. The pulpit and other parts of the chapel were draped in black. The entire service—prayers, hymns, lessons, and sermon—had•reference to the sad events of week. The preacher announced as his text Psalm xc. 12," So teach us to number our days that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." The events of the past week were, he said, full of interest, and painful

div.head: Y ;23, 1892.
div.p: interpretation of it? Perhaps, by-and-by, this also will be made plain; but in the meantime it must be regarded as strange providence. Of the private character of the deceased Prince, and what he was to his own family, it is not for us to speak, but as heir presumptive to the throne of this great empire his public career concerned us all. The high hopes that were centred in him, the great possibilities that lay before him, the exalted sta- tion he seemed destined to all, these all serve to em- phasise the pathos and sadness of his loss, making it one of the most Memorable events of our time. Whatever else this sudden bereavement may mean for the nation, we cannot be wrong in saying that it is a loud call to all of us to set our mind on the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth. At the conclusion of the service the congregation remained standing while the organist (Mr. B. Wadsworth) played the " Dead March" in "Saul."

div.head: ST. MARY'S ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH.
div.p: ST. MARY'S ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH.

In the c-Q:s7; of his -se;in(;ti- lessons of the week," the Rev. M. E. Duggan, 0.5.8., thus referred to the deaths of the Duke of Clarence and Cardinal Man- ning :—ln the last few days death has wandered from the hamlets of the poor, and made its imperious pre- sence felt amid the highest and noblest and most illus- trious of our land. Amid scenes of regal splendour, beneath the very shadow of the throne, it has claimed a victim. Then death sought another victim. But this time it was the high ecclesiastic, the aged Cardinal, weighed down with years of hard, vigorous, and useful I work. His task was finished, his toil was over, and it was but meet that he should, ere long, go to his reward. But his energy, and his wisdom, and his powerful indi- viduality we can with difficulty spare. We may recall the time when he sacrificed a bright future, turned his back on the friends of his youth and manhood, severed every social tie to follow the dictates of his conscience, and entered, as a lowly disciple, the church that he loved so well and served so faithfully. And, when high ecclesiastical honours were imposed upon him, and he took his stand at the head of the English Catholic Hier- archy, we know how strenuously he used his powerful voice and pen in the cause of liberty and justice. He brought forth from its comparative obscurity in these realms the church of his adoption. He made our holy religion respected and revered, and by applying its high principles to the great question of labour, he brought about such arrangements as were just and honourable to both employer and employed. The service concluded with the Dead March in " Saul." THE PARISH CHURCH.

On Sunday the pulpit, reading desk, and altar table of the Parish Church were draped in black, and a sermon based on the word*" Thou shalt be missed, because thy seat will be empty," was preached by the Rev. C. E. Jackson, senior curate, who also referred to the great loss which 'had been sustained by Cardinal Manning's death. Henry Edward Manning, be remarked, was of the people. A typical English schoolb-I, he developed into the typical Englishman. His was that singular combination of intense almost ascetic spirituality and active life, full of manifold practical far-reaching inter- est in the world. He died an honoured prince of an ancient and proud church, a princedom,to which he was not begotten by accident, but to which he was raised for, his own inherent goodness and powers. What coronet shed such a lustre, so graced the brow of man,' as One so earned? Where there was a wrong to redress, suffering to alleviate, any ministry to exercise, any good work to inaugurate, and noble hearted, unselfish purpose, there the hand, the heart, the will of the Cardinal Archbishop were at work. But the mourning over his departure was dwarfed by the unspeakably sad bereavement under which the Royal family was suffering. It was not too much to say that the death of the Duke of Clarence had cast a shadow upon every threshold, and had tinged with a feeling of sadness every heart where our language was spoken. In the evening, the Rev. F. W. Willis referred to the death of the Duke of Clarence. His death, he said, had caused intense sadness._ He was young, and had the best of prospects, and was shortly to have been married. His education had heen well looked after,he having been trained in the navy, university, and army. His charac- ter was blameless, he was manly, and he was abste- mious, scarcely touching wine for dinner. His friends were not rash and riotious, but thdse from whose intel- lectual conversation and advice he would benefit. His death taught them the lesson that God had no favou- rites, and he was sure that their sympathy would go out to his distressed relatives and the Princess Mary of Teck.

div.head: ST. PAUL'S CHURCH.
div.p: ST. PAUL'S CHURCH.

The pulpit of this church on Sunday morning was occupied by the Rev. H. W. Jones, curate of St. Mary's Hulme, Manchester, but the preacher made no reference to the death of the Duke of Clarence. At the conclusion of the service, however, the organist, Mr. J. J. Lythgoe played the dead March in "Saul," the congregation standing as he did so. In the evening a sermon was preached by the Rev. C. V. Merriman, rector of St. Mary's, Hulme, who briefly alluded to the death of his Royal Highness. It was, the preacher urged, always their duty to show sympathy towards those who were in distress, and it was particularly_ their duty to do so on the present occasion, when the Royal fattily were in such deep sorrow. At the conclusion of the service, the Dead March in "Saul "was again played on the organ.
TilE LATE CAItDINAL MANNING.
LORD WOLSELEY'S ATTACHMENT. General Lord Wolseley has replied as follows to a correspondent :

Januay 18, 1892. Dear Sir,—All who knew Cardinal Marnning personally were attached to him. The grace and charm of his manner drew all people to hin4 and the earnestness with which he pleaded for the poor, and especially for the workingman, the basis of all our national wealth, endeared him to all who knew him. Those who had not the advantage of a personal acquaintance with his Eminence admired his efforts in the cause of humanity. He had a big heart, full of human sympathy, and hsa- venly goodness. A sincere Protestant myself; I always felt it a privilege to be in his company, and I deeply valued the prayers which more than once he told me he offered up for me. When shall we see his like again ? Very faithfully yours, Womurt. THE QUEEN, THE PRINCE, AND THE CARDINAL. In reply to messages from the "Vicar Capitular and Chapter of the Archdiocese of Westminster," the follow- ing telegrams have been received : To the Right Rev. Monsignor Gilbert, 22, Finsbury-circus, E.C. • The Queen is very grateful for the kind message of sympathy transmitted by your Chapter, and commands me to convey to you her sincere condolence on the death of Cardinal Manning, whose death her Majesty deeply deplores.—Poxsosurr. The Princess and I deeply appreciate and are very grateful for the warm sympathy expressed by the Chap- ter of the Archdiocese of Westminster, on their own be- half and on behalf of the clergy of the diocese. I had the pleasure of a close acquaintance with Cardinal Man- ning, and found him always a most loyal and stea.ly friend and supporter of the Royal Family. I greatly re- gret his Eminence's loss, and am deeply touched by the kind words he used about my dear son.—ALBERT EDWARD.

TRADE MARA

The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton (vicar) preached in the above church on Sunday morning from the words " Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on thee." In the course of his sermon the rev. gentleman remarked that he thought their hearts, in common with all classes in the country, were with the Prince and Princess of Wales and their family in the very great bereavement which had fallen upon their hluse. He thought they could not that morning better express their sympathy with the bereaved father and mother and their children, in their:great affliction, than by praying that they might find in him the consolation and strength which would enable them to bear it. All such visitations were lessons to them Of the uncertainty of human life. The" Dead March" in Saul was played on the organ at the conclusion of the service, which had been of a very impressive character. EMMANUEL REFORMED CHURCH. At Emmanuel Reformed Church of England, Bold-st., the Rev. Edward P. Reed took for his teat Isa. bd., 1-3, and referred to the death of the Royal Prince.
OTHER REFERENCES. References were also made to the death of the Duke of Clarence at several other churches and chapels in War- rington and the neighbourhood.

John Goodall, described as a local preacher, was remanded at Tamworth, on Monday, on a charge of feloniously assaulting a married woman named Mary Ann Siddals, in a train near Tamworth on Monday week. • Fire broke out on Monday in a cotton warehouse, known as Winder's, between Vandries and Vulcan- streets, Vauxhall-road. Liverpool, and damage esti- mated at £25,000 was caused. The damage is under- stood to be covered by insurance.

An Englishman named Henry Dowd is in custody at New York, on a charge of murdering a lawyer named John Carson. He has confessed to a number of other similar crimes, and the New York police believe that he may ultimately prove to be Jack the Ripper.

THE FUNERAL.

The funeral of Cardinal Manning took place in London on Thursday in a dense fog. A large assembly gathered at the Oratory to attend the solemn requiem mass pre- ceding the burial of the remains of the late Cardinal at Kensal Green Cemetery. The three hours' service at the Oratory commenced at eleven, o'clock, the Bishop of Clifton being the celebrant. The sermon was preached by the Bishop of Newport, and the large church was crowded, amongst those pre- sent being a representative of the Royal family, also the Duke of Norfolk, the Marquis of Bute, Lord Howard of Glossop, Viscount Fielding, Baroness Burdett-Coutts, Sir Charles Russell, Mr. Justin McCarthy, Mr. William O'Brien, Mr. J. Dillon, &c. Fourteen Catholic Bishops were present, and every Caaholic religious body in England was represented by many of the leading mem- bers. The •Spanish Ambassador and othel foreign re- presentatives attended. There was a densely crowded congregation, although admission was by ticket. The service throughout was solemn and impressive. During the service the coffin rested upon a catafalque in front of the high altar. At the close of the service the congregation streamed out into the foggy street, where a vast crowd was await- ing the start of the funeral procession to the cemetery. The dockers had not forgotten their friend,and,with the Cardinal's "body guards," and members of the various temperance bodies, and the Irish National League, were drawn up in readiness to follow the hearse. 'Upwards of 300 carriages were in the procession, 60 be- ing filled by the clergy. The Queen and the Prince of Wales were both represented at the funeral. The Kensal Green Cemetery gave signs of activity at an early hour. People commenced to pour into the cemetery at eleven o'clock. The cemetery was reached late in the afternoon. The coffin was borne straight to the grave, which is of an ordinary character, lined with briar, and near to the late Prinei Lucien Bonaparte's. The ceremony at the grave was a brief one, commenc- ing with the Benedictus, chanted by the priests, and concluding with a prayer for the repose of his 'soul, followed by the sprinkling of holy water. SERVICE AT WARRINGTON.

_ At St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church, on Thursday morning a solemn Requiem Mass was celebrated for the repose of the soul of the late Cardinal Manning. The Rev. T. B. Feeny, 0.5.8., rector of St. Alban's Bewsey- street, officiated as high priest, assisted by the Rev Fathers Craven and M. E. Duggan. A catafalque was erected ia the chancel, covered with a pall, and the high altar was draped in mourning. Father Feeny- gave the absolutions at the catafalque, the burial service being read at the end of the Mass. The music was Novello's, the choir being under the leadership of Mr. Eccles and the organist being Mr. Thos. Mather. The service concluded with the playing of the" Dead March "in " Saul" byMr. Mather. There was a large congregation.

div.head: ST. HELENS AND THE r ATE CARDINAL.
div.p: ST. HELENS AND THE r ATE CARDINAL.

Thursday Gounod's requiem mass was sung at Lowe House Catholic Church, in memory of Cardinal Manning. The church was draped in black, and there was a large congregation. The service was conducted by the Rev. Father Brown, Rector,who was assisted by the Rev. Fathers Toohey and Foley. Mr. Oswald Barton played the Dead March.—At Holy Cross and Sacred Heart masses were also said for the Cardinal. At the latter chtrch Mr. Williams also played the Dead March.

div.head: FIGHTING IN PERSIA.-280 KILLED.
div.p: FIGHTING IN PERSIA.-280 KILLED.

Serious fighting has occurred in the Persian district of Balladash between the inhabitants, who have been roused to revolt by the priests, and the Government troops sent against them. Two hundred of the rebels were killed, while the troops had eighty killed and ninty wounded.

div.head: LABOUR COMMISSION.
div.p: THE LABOUR COMMISSION.

The business of the Labour Commission was resumed, on Wednesday, when evidence was given on behalf of the Lanarkshire miners, who were said to be unanim- ously in favour of an eight hours' day. Complaint was made as to the conditions under which the men laboured, one of the most serious grievances being the question of housing. It was stated that a third of the cottages occupied by the miners were owned by employers, who charged rather high rents.

Increase in 50 years 13,037,000 It will be seen from these figures that, while the Population of England and Wales has increased nearly 100 per cont, during the last half century, the Population of Ireland has decreased over 40 per cent. As a matter of fact the Po. pulation of Ireland to-day is actually less than it was in 1800, when the Act of Union was passed 1337 Means the most infamous in English history. There need be no fear, then,of Irishmen still further leaving their country when they are free to govern themselves. The idea is absurd. On the contrary, B°lne of the tens of thousands of pounds which are Se t by the Irish people from the United States and other countries to enable their relatives to leave their homes will be employed in taking Irish- run back to those homes. This reversal of opera- tions will affect England as well as America ; the labour market of both countries will be relieved in- atead of glutted; and it is safe, therefore, to say ttsliat the English workman who votes for Home T'ule votes in favour of his own improvement, while uelPing on a measure which will enable Irishmen t° live and thrive in their own country.

The Jr seems to be settled that the Influenza peculiar malady known as in- Scourge. fluenza has its origin, like con- 41117°Ption, in a specific microbe, but it is not yet settled how the microbe is to be exterminated. ,n4eting on the time-honoured adage that " pre- -I:ention is better than care," various experimvnts have been made, and some of them seem to have , .„,..ueen attended with considerable success. Dr. F. vv• Corby, writing to the "British Medical Jour- a!" gives a simple preventive which, he says," up '() the present has not failed in stopping the pro- -I,grese of infection in any household in which it has "een tried. The prophylactic is composed of equal Parta of pure carbolic acid and glycerine of which two or three drops should be dropped on the hand- kerchiefl_ .. in use every morning before leaving the "mroom." Similar to this is the advice given by .rtain Edinburgh physicians who say that "the M " preventive is to put a few drops of eucalyptus 1:)!I on one's pocket handkerchief daily." So far as lulplicity goes this plan may be said to be more exquisite than the other," and at the pro- le!" t moment it is being tried extensively. "TOUCH AND GO."
We hold over several letters, and report of Penketh Liberal tea meeting held last night.

Bury " wasn't in it," on Saturday, in the com- petition in connection with the National Physical Recreation Society. The win was an extraordin- ary one, with a total score of 303 points t 3 223. However, the winners must not be content to say to the defeated team—" Go 'bury' thy sorrows." They must prepare for a stiffer contest in the next round, and for a final victory.

The shop assistants of Warrington are making another attempt to secure a half-holiday, and it is to be hoped they will this time be successful. Would it not be pc 3sible to get a joint conference of shopkeepers and shopmen ? If that could be done, the rest might prove to be plain sailing. It should not be forgotten that employers as well as employed require relaxation ; and unity of action means that the boon would be general.

The late Mathew Arnold (or was it Mr. W. Mor- ris?) once described such towns as Widnes and St. Helens as" hell-holes." Canon Eyre, formerly of St. Helens, has, as will be seen from another column,been comparing the place to Pandemoniun, referring in particular to the men who have to work half-naked at the glass manufactories. Some of them—good-natured as they were—be- come" perfect devils" through drinking to excess. St. Helens has evidently made a strong impres- sion upon Canon Eyre.

The Tories are under obligation to deal with education in Ireland, and the Home Secretary has admitted that it will be "a cause of some difficul- ties for the Government." This, added to the difficulties of the promised Local Government Bill for Ireland, is suggestive of a lively session. This comes of course of shirking duty ; there is death- bed repentisnce,and hope at the last moment to be "saved by works." The faith of the Government, or faith in the Government, is now out of the question. •

There is a rift within the lute of the Unionists, and not all that comes therefrom is harmony. Mr. Chamberlain's son Austen is on the cards as a can- didate for East Worcestershire; but " a resolution adopted at the meeting of the committee was sub- mitted, requiring Mr. A. Chamberlain to pledge himself not to support measures calculated to in- jure the Unionist Government." This has irritated Mr. Chamberlain, for it means that the Chamber- lains are not to be trusted unless they "take the pledge." How about "the union of hearts" in this case

There was an excellent record of good work done at the first annual meeting, on Tuesday, of the Earlestown and District Medical Aid Society. Having secured a large stock of medical appliances, it was resolved to appeal for subscriptions to secure the services of a trained nurse. There should be no difficulty about raising a sufficient sum if collections are made at the various works and at churches and chapels. Contributors will then be able to say with Wordsworth : The primal duties shine aloft, like stars ; The charities that sootb, and heal, and bless, Are scattered at the feet of man, like flowers.

It is stated that when Mr. John Redmond, M.P., found that he had lost his one-hundred guinea presentation watch, at the Dublin demonstration, on Saturday, he immediately put his hand to the chain from which his watch had previously de- pended, and holding it up to the crowd, asked that the gentleman who had taken the watch should return it to him. It seems that Mr. Redmond saves all his hard words for Irish patriots; and that when he has to deal with a thief he is— the mildest mannered man That ever scuttled ship, or cut a throat. However, the "gentleman "in this case turned a deaf ear. The police have since laid hands on him, but as to the watch nothing can be found of it except bits of the broken case.

Mr. Robert Pierpoint let the cat out of the bag on Tuesday evening. Speaking, as the Tory can- didate for Warrington, upon Ireland and Home Rule, he said :—" The utmost hatred now existed and the utmost warfare had taken place between the religious parties in Ireland, and the Protest- ants of Ulster were deadly opposed to it. Ulster was the most prosperous and ir dustrious part of Ireland, and were they going to hand over their Protestant brethren to the tender mercies of the Roman Catholics in Ireland ?"

Catholics who are asked to vote for the Tory candidate will please to have the above in mind. It means that,in the opinion of Mr. Pierpoint,they are not to be trusted to act fairly, if power be given their brethren in Ireland. But why wasn't this said in 1885, when Sir Gilbert Greenall talked about " autonomy "for Ireland, and moved heaven and earth to secure the Catholic vote ? As to trl—,er, what is meant is this—that, although the Orangemen are in a minority, they must continue to dominate the majority. That is Tory exclusive- nees, and Warrington Catholics are expected to vote for it.

By-the-bye what are the answers which Mr. Pierpoint has given to the five questions which were, we presume, put by the Orangemen to him, as they were put to Sir Gilbert Greenall ? And what are the quesuions themselves ? Have they anything to do with voting for an inquiry into, or inspection of nunneries? There should be no secrecy in a matter of this kind. The Orangemen of Warrington are pledged to vote for Mr. Pier- point, and they are not pledged for nothing. "Brother Bloomfield" said there were 800 of them, but that was a bit of "Brother Bloomfield's " blarney. They will have to be all counted to find 150 good on the hooks. Still the main point is— whatquestions have the Orangemen put, and what are Mr. Pierpoint's answers ?

The new sixpenny magazine "The Idler " edited by Mr. Jerome K. Jerome and Mr. Robert Barr—is out, and may he said to be more than "up to date," for the first number,dated February, reaches us in the middle of January. It is an al- together " forward " bantling,and ought to thrive, nursed as it is by Mark Twain Bret Harte, Andrew Lang,James Payne,Luke Sharp and other notabilities. The new magazine is certainly strong both in text and illustration. An extraordinary featina is a series of blended portraits—actual re- sults of photography--showing,in one instance,the composite face of Salisbury-Smith-Balfour-Gos- chen ; in another Gladstone-Harcourt-Rosebery- Morley ; and finally one composeA of the whole eight. The effect is certainly striking and sug- gestive.
HYDROPHOBIA OR BLOOD POISONING? SINGULAR

DBATH AT Sr. HIMMEL On Saturday, Mr. S. Brighouse held an inquest at the St. Helens Town Hall on the body of Alfred Radcliffe, 13 years of age, son of William Radcliffe, a labourer, of 48, Llwrenson's-terrace, off Cyril-st., who clf ed under singular circumstances on Tuesday night.—The Coroner remarked that there was some doubt whether the boy had died from the effects of hydrophobia or from blood poisoning. The evidence showed that on the 18.1 December the boy was pass- ing along Eccleston-street when. he was bitten on the left knee by a terrier dog. The skin was broken, and there was some slight bleeding. The injury was bathed and poulticed, and apparently healed in two or three days. A. fortnight ago, however, it was found that the boy had a small scar on his left ankle, but there was no evidence as to how he re- ceived it. The ankle began to swell, and the boy suffered from pains in the leg. The father and mother stated that he drank a great quantity of water, and occasionally snapped and attempted to bite those near him. Dr. Grey was called in last Monday,but the boy died on Tuesday night. —ln his evidence Dr. Grey said he found the boy suffering from blood-poisoning and he never noticed any symptoms of hydrophobia.—The Coroner: Then in your opinion, the bite of the dog had nothing to do with the death of the boy? Witness: No.— The Coroner; You think that the cause of death was blood-poisoning from the wound on the ankle? —Witness. Yee. Pneumonia supervened on the blood-poisoning.—The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical evidence. Krratule RANGERS.—GarIand Builders Ironmonger, War ringtose: act

RUNCORN FR Ell PUBLIC LIBRARY.

During the past mouth 1,824 books have been issued from this library, being an increase of 50 over the cor- responding month last year. LACEY-ST., BAND OF HOPE, WIDNES. This society gave a public entertainment on Monday evening,when a programme of songs, recitations, &c., was creditably gone through. Mr. W. Hodgkinson pre- sided.
EVENINGS FOR THE PEOPLE AT WIDNES.
At the National Schools, on Thursday evening, Mr. J. A. Thompson, of Liverpool, delivered a lecture on the re- markable life of the late Bishop Crowther, which was listened to by a large audience.
ALBERT-ROAD CHAPEL, WIDNES.

In aid of the funds of this place the Rev. J. Wardle Stafford preached an eloquent sermon to a large con- gregation on Thursday afternoon. In the evening he delivered a lecture on" Darkest England and the way out." There was a good audience. • BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN. At the weekly meeting on Wednesday, Mr. T. Hart- land, of Widnes, read a paper on "The House of Lords; shall it be ended or mended." The essayist strongly ad- vocated the ending of the second chamber, and tho majority of the members agreed with him.

div.head: Tan LAT& REV. C. R. RAMSHANY.
div.p: Tan LAT& REV. C. R. RAMSHANY.

Our readers will learn with regret that the Rev. C. R. Ramshaw, United Methodist Free Church minister,who was formerly stationed at Runcorn, died very suddenly at Longton a week ago. He had preached the day be- fore his death at Dresden in the Potteries. He had been in the ministry about forty years.

ST. AMBROSE CHURCH, TEIIIPERANCE SOCIETY, WIDNES. The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday evening, when the Rev. J. R. Glover, curate, delivered an address on" Temperance." A capital musical entertainment was given by a number of the members. The Rev. G. A. be Best presided. On Wednesday evening, the juvenile branch was treated to a limelight exhibition by Mr. G. Rae, of Bold. The views were illustrative of Wales.

div.head: AGED PEOPLE'S TREAT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: AGED PEOPLE'S TREAT AT RUNCORN.

The arrangements for this annual treat to the old folk are now nearly completed, and the promoters expect to have about 500 to dinner in the Public Hall on Wednesday evening. The bill of fare will consist of savoury hot pot and mince tarts, with tea or coffee, at the wish of the guests; and before leaving each old woman will receive a packet of tea and each old man a packet of tobacco. After dinner an entertainment will be given, and Mr. John Allen, of the Minnehaha Minstrels, the well-known stump orator and comic vocalist, will occupy a considerable portion of the pro- gramme. A number of local vocalists will also take part. The proceedings commence at 5 o'clock.

RUNCORN WOMEN'S TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION. On Wednesday evening„a most successful tea meeting, under the auspices of the above society, was held in Bethesda Lecture Hall. Over 300 people sat down to an excellent tea. The tables were presided over by Mesdames Cullis, Bellamy, Cooke, Smith, Green, T. Simpkin, J. D. Jones, P. Leathwood, D. Bisbrown, Newall, Weston, Jones, Clarke, F. J. Norman, Martin, Millinger, and Gandy, and the Misses Simist.er, Crosby, Norman, A. Littler. A. Jones, and Williams. After tea, a public meeting was held, under the presidency of the Rev. W. Arrowsmith,who in an admirable address spoke of the noble work of the Women's Temperance Associa- tion, and the need of such an organisation, pointing out the misery and wretchedness resulting from the use of intoxicating liquors. Mrs. Ecroyde, of Liverpool, a member of the U.K.A., delivered a most forcible and earnest speech on women's work in relation te temper- ance, and her remarks had a practical effect on the audience, many pledges being taken at the end of the meeting. The musical portion of the meeting was undcr the management of Mr. Robert Yates.

REATIL AND FUNERAL OP AM OLD RUNCORN RESIDENT. Mrs. Brookes, widow of the late Mr. John Brookes, formerly manager of the Weston Stone Quarries, died on Saturday morning last, at the residence of her son- in-law, Mr. F. Beck, West Bank, Frodsham. The de- ceased lady, who was highly nspected, had reached the advanced age of 80 years. The funeral took place on Wednesday, when her mortal remains were laid beside ' two husbands in a grave in Bethesda Congregational I Churchyard, at Runcorn. Before leaving Frodsham a service was conducted at the Union Church by the Rev. Mr. Craddock, and on arriving at Runcorn the soffin was placed in a hearse supplied by Messrs. Yarwood Bros., and the two coaches which followed contained the following mourners :—Mr. Wm. Brookes (son), Mr.Thos. Handley (son-in-law), Messrs. Wm. Chadwick, John Beck (grandson), J. B. Chadwick and J. B. Handley (grand- son),Mrs. Evans, and Miss Maggie Beck. The cortege was met at the church by Messrs. J. R. Frith, W. Handley, W. Sutton, W. Ladynaan, John Bate, and H. W. Hand- ley. The carriers were Messrs. Samuel Walker and John Smith (Weston Quarries), and Messrs. Philip Booth, and Joseph Lightfoot, Handley, and Beck. The solemn service at the graveside was conducted by the Rev. John Simpson.

A LECTURE ON BEEKEEPING AT FARNWORTIL On Monday evening a lecture on the above subject was delivered in the Farnworth National Schools, by Mr. Harbordt, Mr. T. Snape, C.C., in the chair. There was a large audience. Mr. Snape said that a friend of his at Widnes had asked him what he knew about "bee- keeping." He must admit that he had no practical ex- perience in beekeeping, but the chief reason why he was present that evening was to represeat the Lanca- shire County Council, as he was chairman of the Tech- nical Instruction Committee of the Lancashire County Council. Amongst the numerous applications which they had-for grants in aid of technical education, one was from the Lancashire and Cheshire Beekeepers' Asso- ciation,for a grant for the purpose of extending the cul- ture of beekeeping. After some discussion, they had decided to give a grant of £lOO for this purpose. He said that if the farmers were wise they would use every means of increasing their capital, for in these days of keen competition one had to be alive if he was going to succeed, and one means by which farmers could assist themselves was by keeping bees. Mr. Ilarbordt, of the Lancashire and Cheshire Beekeepers' Association then delivered his lecture, dealing on the management of bees, and their general habits, &c. The lecture was pro- fusely illustrated by the aid of a lantern, and proved very interesting. The usual votes of thanks closed the meeting. FUNERAL OF MRS. TI7.IMtNS, OF RUNCORN.

The programme will be provided by Mr. Josef Cantor's Gems of the Opera's Company, which has won golden opinions in many parts of Lancashire, and the en- tertainment will be of a varied and most enjoyable character.

STEALING AT RUNCORN.

On Wednesday,at Runcorn Police Court,before Messrs. J. Handley and G. L. Davies, Mary Ellen Walker, aged 14 years, was charged with stealing a purse containing half a sovereign,from the house of Henry Riva,Portland- st. The Bench decided to deal with the prisoner under the First Offenders' Act, and the father was bound over in RS to bring up his daughter for judgment when called upon. UNIVERSITY EXTRNSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN.

The second of the series of on the History of Florence, by the Rev. W. Hudson Shaw will be delivered in Bethesda Lecture hall on Monday evening. The sub- ject will be Dante. It is hoped that the towspeople :will show their appreciation of the imports,pce of the subject and of the efforts of the Cotninittee'"to continue the provision of the means of intellectual advancement, by attending the lectures in large numbers.
A RUNCORN DOCTOR AND His FBRS.

At Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, Mr. E. Wors- ley held an inquest on the body of Mary Wood, a single woman 28 years of age, who had lived at 61, Percival- lane. It appeared that the woman was confined of twins a short time ago and was apparently recovering nicely until Friday, when she had a relapse. Dr. Man- gan who was sent for refused to attend the case unless his fee of Sc. was paid. The woman died before the messenger returned.--Several of the jury spoke strongly with respect to Dr. Mangan's refusal to attend the case, ' but the Coroner said a medical man was not compelled to attend a case without payment cf the usual fees.—A verdict of death from natural causes was returned. DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MRS. ANDERSON OF THE RAIL- WAY HOTEL, WIDNES. Mrs. Anderson, landlady of the Railway Hotel, Widnes, died on Saturday at the early age of 42 years. The deceased was of a very genial and kindly disposi- tion and ever ready to help the distressed. Her mortal remains were interred at Farnworth churchyard on Wednesday afternoon, and the funeral was of an impos- ing character. The Committee and a number of the , members of Widnes Football Club, each carrying a wreath, headed the mournful procession; then followed deputations from the Widnes Tradesmen's Football and , Cricket Club; the Operative Society of Bricklayers; and the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants. Then came the hearse, and 20 coaches, containing the relatives and friends of the decoased. The funeral ser- vice was conducted by the Rev. G. H. Garrett, B.D. T. & W. HATING MATCH, A Sr. HELBNI3 MA.N DEFBATID. A skating match for a cup valued at £55 came off, on Saturday afternoon, in the presence of a large concourse of people on Sefton meadows. The con- testants were Fred Litherland, of Sefton, holder of the quarter-mile skating championship of England, and John Highcock, of St. Helens. The distance covered was a quarter of a mile,and the tracks were in good condition. After two attempts, I3oth men ' get away to a good start, a strong wind blowing with them. When 120 yards had been covered Litherland was seen to have the beat of the race, and he got home an easy winner by 30 yards in the remarkably short space of time of 35 1-5 seconds, the finish of the race creating a great deal of excite- ment. A considerable number of persons accom- panied Highcock from S. Helens and backed his chances for large sums, which, much to their chag- rin, they had to leave behind them, Litherland's fine display greatly upsetting their calculations. HAS FITTINGS.-4. S. Garland, Gas Fitter, Bridge-st., Warrlngton.—Advt.

A ST. HELENS GIRL WA.SHXD AWAY. The body of Mary Ann Tracy, 15 years of age, daughter of Patrick Tracey, a labourer, of Stone-st., St. Helens, was found in the Sankey Brook, near the Havanna Colliery, Parr, on Tuesday night. On the 10th of December last several girls, including Tracey, were picking up cinders from the waste heaps near to Baxter's Chemical Works. The girls attempted to cross the swollen Sankey Brook by means of a plank bridge, and all succeeded in doing so with the exception of the deceased, who was blown into the water by the gusty wind, and her body was washed down the stream. Attempts were made to recover the body by the use of grapnling irons, but without success. On Tuesday night a workman passing along the side of the brook saw a body "jammed "against the stump of an old tree, and on being got to the side it was found to be that of the missing girl. The body was removed to the Ship Inn, Newton Common, awaiting an inquest. J. W. DtrrToses AIanLAL WINTER SALE is now on. Sankey-st.--Advt.

It has now been definitely arranged that the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, arid North Lancashire Agricul- tural Show of 1892, will be held on July 21st, 22nd, and 2.lrd. Entries will be received up to the end of June.

TREAT TO AGED PEOPLE AT WIDNES. The first treat to the aged people of Widnes took place in the Lacey-st. School on Thursday evening, and the three hundred who assembled,spent a most enjoyable time together. The credit of initiating the movement belongs to Supt. Keighley, but the idea, once mooted, was heartily taken up, and a commit- tee of at least 60 members was formed to deal with the affair. Supt. Keighley was elected chairman, Mr. H. Singleton treasurer, and Mr. F. J. Poole secretary. The appeal for subscriptions met with a ready response from the public, and about £lOO was obtained, of which a con- siderable surplus is left after treating the old people generously, and to what use this must be put will be considered in a few days. The age limit was fixed at 60 years, and invitations were sent to over 400 people, the oldest being a woman 91 years of age, but she was unfortunately not able to attend the treat, and this old lady and others in similar circumstances were provided for at their homes. The repast consisted of ham and beef sandwiches and fancy cakes, and after tea, each person was presented with lib. of tea or fib. of tobacco according to choice. A musical entertainment was given by the following local vocalists :—Misses Leather- barrow, Miss L. White. Messrs. J. R. Lea, G. J. Neil, J. Morrison, T. Smith, and A. Evans.—An exhibition of ' legerdemain and ventriloquism by Professor Wyman was a prominent feature. Mr. W. White and Mr. J. Caldwell ably officiated as accompanists. Major Wareing presided over the proceedings in the unavoid- able absence of Mr. Gossage, and said no meeting ha had ever attended in Widnes had given him so much pleasure as that. Dr. O'Keefe proposed a vote of thanks to the trustees for the free use of the school, to Mrs. Deacon for the loan of plants,and to the people of Widnes who had contributed so liberally to the treat.—Mr. F. H. Pankhurst seconded, and the motion was carried unanimously. On the motion of Superintendent Kaigh- ley, seconded by Mr. D. Wright, a vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman.—As the guests left the hall, each received a parcel of provisions.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RETNCORN, &c.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RETNCORN, &c.
"By AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."

1 Public bodies are said to possess no consciences, but Widnes School Board appears to be an excep- tion to that rule. For eight years they have been trying to pay an account of about £7O for the supply of a boiler to one of their schools, but the contrac- tor treats their request for an account with silent indifference, and at last, made desperate, the Board have decided to notify him that unless the desired bill is forthcoming they will take advantage of the Statute of Limitation and refuse to pay the money. I should like to know that contractor; he is unique amongst his class.

The School Board rate of Widnes is gradually creep- ing up to a high figure. Last year the Board received £3,900 from the rates,this year they demand £4,500, an increase of no less than £6OO, for which repairs to the several schools are largely responsible. It is a fact that in Widnes buildings soon fall to rack and ruin if not continually attended to, and the I Board are pursuing a wise policy in keeping them in thoroughly good condition. The fact is that if the schools are to be kept efficient we must expect the rata to increase, and, as Mr. Timmis pointed out, the present increase should not press hardly, as parents have been relieved of the payment of school fees to the extent of .£3,000 per annum. Let us hope that they will soon be relieved of the whole burden of school fees.

As to what will be the amount of the School Board rate is surrounded by some mystery. The Chairman stated it at 9d.; Major Wareing at 7d.; and the overseers, observed the Major, will probably place it at Sad. Of course the Major is right, taking the gross rateable value, which he is perfectly entitled to do, but the various reductions allowed considerably reduce the total, and it is highly prob- able that the actual rate will be near the Chairman's figure. Theory and practice dont seem to agree in this instance.

The death of the Duke of Clarence if it has cast a gloom over this neighbourhood, has evoked univer- sal sympathy with the Royal Family in their great bereavement. At the public buildings the flags have been hoisted half mast, and on Wednesddy the day of the funeral, many windowswere darkened in recognition of the sad event. On Monday next the Runcorn Board of Commissioners will hold a special meeting for the purpose of passing a vote of condolence to her Majesty, and with the Prince and Princess of Wales.

The plans of a Technical Institute for Runcorn have been adopted, but it is perfectly clear that un- less the grants obtained in aid are very large, the building will not be proceeded with on the scale at present proposed. Now,a glance at the plans would convince anyone that the building is none too large for the purpose intended, if the teaching is to be effi- cient and the pupils are to study with comfort. There is one room set apart for art students to sketch from life, which I think is scarcely needed, and would suggest should be added to the chemical laboratory, which is too small for a town where the staple trade is chemicals, and where those desirous of studying that fascinating science might be ex- pected to be the most numerous class. Unfortu- nately for Mr. Pritchard's scheme,the land he men- tions has been appropriated for School Board exten- sion, and, besides,he was rather late in the day with his suggestion. The only difficulty in the way of the Commissioners' scheme is the cost, and if it is to be carried out there will have to he generous subscriptions from those interested in the town and who can afford to give. There is a thousand pounds waiting to be taken from Mr. Brunner,and so far no effort has been made to obtain it. Up to now Mr. Philip Speakman is the only voluntary subscriber to the Institute who will swell the list.

The contract for the new. Post Office and other buildings on Savage's Bridge, Runcorn, has been let by Mr. Speakman to Messrs. W. Farrell and Son, and a start will be made in erecting the structures as soon as possible.

I hear that Mr. Weston, formerly in charge of the Runcorn and Weston sections of the Ship Canal has in conjunction with another gentleman, succeeded in obtaining the contract for the contruction of the Wrexham and Ellesmere Railway. This is the second important contract Mr. Weston has secured since he commenced business as a contractor.

The resolutions from the Widnes Trades Council with respect to the letting of municipal contracts have received scant consideration from the local authorities of Runcorn and Widnes. At both places the communication has been ignored by being "laid on the table." Possibly those authorities may not always ignore the representations of the Council, which has within itself the form of a powerful organisation of workingmen, whom the Local Board of Widnes and the Board of Commis- sioners are supposed to represent. There is surely nothing alarming in the request that, contracts shall be given to firms of good standing and paying the recognised standard of wages, rather than to a contractor who marks his profit by " sweating" his employs.

The giving of a contract to the lowest tenderer is frequently a penny wise and pound foolish proceed- ing, as both the Boards in question know to their. cost in more than one instance. 1 should advise the Trades Council not to be content with one repulse but to risk another. The eve of an election might find the members in a more compliant mood.

Mr. John Beech made his first appoarance as a member of Widnes Local Board, last week, and it was evident that he intended not only ;.o be seen, but frequently heard. He ventured where more experienced members refrained from treading, and like Don Quixote, when he had a tilt with the windmill, met with a decided repulse. He objected to the raising of the salary of the matron of the Cottage Hospital to the modest sum of .£4O, for the not very cogent reason that the town was about to be incorporated ; and the trades- people will bear him in remembrance for his sug- gestion that they should. be compelled to keep the parapet clear of snow in times like the present. With regard to his question as to Mr, Brown's quali- fication, it would have been better had he made some reliable inquiry before introducing the matter at the public board, and it would have come with better grace had he given the gentleman most in- terested, notice that he would raise such a point. There is room for Mr. Beech's reforming zeal, but he should have, as the saying goes, felt his feet , before he commenced his attack.

A Runcorn gentleman thus describes a reminis- cence of the Duke of Clarence and his brother Prince George in their boyhood's days. "During one of my perigrinations around the British Isles, I had occasion in the year 1878 to pass the Exeter Station. Having to change train, I was walking along the platform, bag in hand, when I received a number of

sharp and smarting blows on the cheek,and looking to my right saw two youngsters standing at the door of a saloon carriage, merrily laughing. " What do you mean, you young rascals ! "I exclaimed,and I was rapidly striding towards them, intent on yen- Renee, when a bystander restrained me, remarking "They are the Prince of Wales's sons going home for their holidays." The Princes were at this time cadets on board the "Britannia," stationed at Dartmouth. The missiles which had struck me were directed by pea shooters with which the boys were provided, and doubtless finding the range of their saloon too short, were trying larger distances wheti halting at railway stations."

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. Mr. T. Sutton Timmis presided, and there were present the Revs. Dean Finegan and Father Clarke, Major Wareing, Dr. O'Keeffe, Mr. G. Wade-Deacon, and Mr. G. H. Danby (clerk).

div.head: DISTRICT EDUCATION.
div.p: DISTRICT EDUCATION.

The District Education Committee reported that dur- ing December (three weeks) there were seven applica- tions for school fees which were recommended to be paid, 228 persons were summoned before the Committee for contravention of the Education Act, and 27 were prosecuted and convicted by the magiitrates.—The re- port was adopted.

div.head: AN APPOINTMENT.
div.p: AN APPOINTMENT.
On the recommendation of the School Management Cornmittee,Mr. Reginald Showan was engaged as an ex- pupil teacher in the senior boys' department of Simms' Cross School, at the rate of £4O per annum.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

The Finance Committee re3omlnended the payment of accounts amounting to £667 18s., which included £4BO for salaries. The receipts for the month had been School fees £47 65.5 d., fee grant from Government £358 55., made up as follows :—Simms' Cross, £165 7s. 6d. ; Warrington-road, £72 17s. 6d. ; and West Bank, £l2O ; other items Making the total receipts £412 6s. ld.—The accounts were passed. A TEAR'S EXPENDITURE. INCREASED RATE. Major Wareing, as chairman, of the Finance Com- mittee submitted the estimate of expenditure of the Board for the year ending September 29th, 1892 : £ s. d.
