Comparing this estimate with that of the previous year, Major Wareing said the school management estimated their requirements at £689, and they had actually spent £BBB 14s. sd. ; the District Education Committee esti- mated £440, and had spent £442 2s. 3d.; the Sites and Building Committee estimated £5OO and had spent £579 15s. Bd.: and the Finance Committee estimated £2,290 and spent £2,146 6s. 3d. These figures showed that the total estimated expenditure was £3,919, and the expen- dittire had been £4,057 19s. 7d., or £157 19s. 7d. ex- pended in excess of the estimates. The balance in th:A bank at the commencement of the year was £304 14s. 6d., and was now £146 14s. 11d. He explained that the school management had received in fees £B5 less than was anticipated, and the increased price of fuel was also the cause of greater expenditure. The salaries of teachers had also been under-estimated. The excess of expenditure over estimate by the Slate and Building Committee was caused by the increased cost of labour, and the damage done to roofs and win- dows by the storm. The present estimates were based upon the past requirements of the coming year, and he enum- erated the work which would have to be undertaken by the Sites and Building Committee which was the cause of the increase in their estimate. He moved that a precept be served upon the Overseers for the sum of £4,500, being the estimated amount of the deficiency in the school fund up to 29th of September, 1892 ; also that the precept be signed and seated, and made payable on or before the Ist day of March, 1892. —The Chairman seconded the motion, and said lie be- lieved it was good policy to keep the property of the Board in good repair. Theymight go on patching and cobbling, and then at the finish there would be an enor- ous expense. He admitted that they were asking for a large sum, and he was so •ry they had to ask for it, but it was necessary to put the finances of the Board on a sound basis. It would be 9d. in the £on the rates, and he sympathised with many ratepayers who would have to pay it, but the smaller ratepayers should not forget that by the fee grant they were relieved of somethinglike £3,000 a year.He therefore thought they might with good grace be asked to pay £5OO more from the rates to put the finances on a sound basis, and to keep the schools in a good state of repair.—Dean Finegan pointed out that in the estimates of the School Management was the sum of £7O for a boiler, Sec., at Warrington-road, which had been fixed about eight years ago. They had been unable to get an account from the contractor, and he suggested that a letter should be written to him demanding a bill, and stating that if it were not rendered, the Board would take advantage ot their legal position and refuse to pay it.—Major Wareing approved of the Dean's sug- gestion, and, referring to the Chairman's statement that the rate would be 9d. in the £, said the rateable value of Widnes, according to the figures of the Local Board, which were the best they could get, was £140,057 10s. and his found that their precept on that basis would require a rate of 7.71 d. in the £. The Overseers made reductions for various reasons and to varying amounts on that rateable value, and the rate would pro- bably be 8.71 d. in the £,but with that the School Board had nothing to do.—Dean Finegan said the Major had been very clear, and there was one thing they must do, and that was not be so easy in raising salaries in future.

div.head: HEAD TBACH-ER'S GRIEVANCE.
div.p: A HEAD TBACH-ER'S GRIEVANCE.

A joint letter was read from Mr. Showan and Mr. Devonald, head teachers, complaining that they had been deprived of payments through the operation of a scheme of salaries which they had not accepted and con- trary to a scheme which they had accepted.—ln reply to Mr. Deacon, Mr. Danby said he thought Mr. Showan had received more under the latter scheme thin he would under the previous one, and he had accepted pay- ments under the scheme he said he had not accepted.— The Chairman said Mr. Showan must not take half of

one scheme and half of another.—The Board approved of the action of the School Management Committee, who had dealt with the matter, and the Clerk was instructed to prepare a return showing what Mr. Sho wan would have received under the old scheme and what he re- ceived under the new scheme.

div.head: LAMOUR CERTIFICATES.
div.p: LAMOUR CERTIFICATES.

The Rev. Dean Finegan and Mr. Deacon were ap- pointed a deputation to attend a confereace in London on the 27th inst., arranged by the Leeds School Board, also to for • part of a deputation to the Education De- partment with regard to the granting oE labour certifi- cates.

div.head: SONS OF TEMPERANCE GRAND DIVISION OF CHESHIRE. ANNUAL SESSION.
div.p: SONS OF TEMPERANCE GRAND DIVISION OF CHESHIRE. ANNUAL SESSION.

On Monday, he annual Session of the above order was held at the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Run- corn. There was a full attendance of officers, and a goodly number of representatives present from the various lodges in the district, namely from Chester, Crewe, Runcorn, Weston, Handley, Winsford and Northwich. The Session was opened at 10 o'clock a.m. Mr. Daniel Bisbrown, G.W.P. presided, and in address- ing the Session urged each member to throw all his energies into this work of temperance reform. He pro- ceeded :—There is no blinking the tact that we have reached a crisis in our Grand Division. Matters of vital import will be brought before your notice to-day, which I will need our most careful consideration ; difficulties must be faced and dealt with once for all. Two schemes recommended after most careful consideration by the committee appointed at our last Grand Division, are of supreme importance. If the Grand Division in its Wisdom refuses to accept this scheme, I see no other alternative but decentralization, and forming a funeral fund, and leyplecaose course o e then each division may give just whattt i their sick members. But, brethren, whatever we take, let us be united,for " United we stand, divided we fall." Let our motto be "In things essential unity— in things doubtful liberty—but in all things charity." We are engaged in a high and noble cause. To save the fallen, and to save others from falling. For we hold that teetotalism is not only good as a theory, but also in practice, not only good to hold and believe in as a senti- ment, but good to carry out in every day life. Conclud- ing the speaker said :—We are on the eve of a General Election; don't let us be found napping. When the day of battle comes, let us throw ourselves in the thick of the fight. The liquor party are on the war path—let us give a good account of ourselves and consecrate our votes to the sacred cause M temperance, and place in the hands of the people the supreme power in regard to the licenses of public-houses—in other words the Direct Veto. (Applause.) X. Thomas Cooke, G. Scribe, then gave a financial

and numerical report of the order in the district for the past year, whilst reports were also given by the depu- ties and representatives of the progress in each of their respective divisions. Mr. T. Heesom, G.P., of Cadets, gave a very encouraging report of the juvenile branch of the order in the district. This being the annual meeting the election of officers took place when the foliewing were duly elected for the next twelve months, namel :—Mr. W. R. Hamilton,of Chester, G.W.P, ; Mr:

Edward Key,. of Runcorn' G. W.A. ; Mr. T. Cooke, of Runcorn, re-elected G. Scribe, Mr. J. Jones,of Runcorn,. G. Treas. : Mr. T. Ford, of Weston, G. Chaplain, Mr. J. T. Yearsley, of Northwich, G. Con. • Mr. W. Heath, oi Crewe, G. Sen. ; Mr. G. F. Adams,of'Chester,and Mr. W. Kennerley, of Winsford, auditors; Mr. E. Key, and Mr. S. M. Temperley,of Runcorn. Book examiners, Messrs. J. Bowering, of Crewe, Mr. T. Heesom, of Runcorn, and Mr. G. Cook, C.C. of Handley, re-elected trustees ; W. Farish Esq., of Helsby, and Messrs. Ainsworth and Hi'- ditch re-elected arbitrators ; Mr. T. Heesom,of Runcorn, re-elected 6.?. of Cadets. and Messrs. T. Ravenscroft,of Weston, J. Hitchen,of Birkenhead, E. Hughes,of Chester, P. Leicester, of Northwich, and H. Hallmark, of Crewe. Committee of management, Mr. Daniel Bisbrown, f Runcorn, and Mr. E.Hughes,of Chester were appointed to attend as representatives of the Grand Division. The annual session of the National Division to be held at Bristol in .Whit week.

_ The following resolutions with several others were then considered, discussed, and adopted : Scale I. " That all members initiated prior to July 18th, 1883, shall pay under Scale 1, is. id. per fortnight Contribu- tions, to be divided as follows :11.d, to the Benefit Fund and 2d. to tbe Management Fund ; and shall be entitled if good upon the books to the following allowance viz. : for the first 26 weeks of such illness, the sum of 12s, weekly ; and should such illness continue, then for the next 26 seeks the sum of 6s. weekly ; and in the event of continued illness, 3s. per week so long as he remains ill. Should any member that has been in receipt of sick pay declare off the funds of the Division, and afterwards declare upon the funds again within the space of 12 ca,lender mouths, from the time of declaring off, he shall be paid according to such part of the above scale as he was in receipt of when he declared off the funds in the previous illnesss ; and should any member be afflicted a second time or any number of times, he shall be entitled to receive the full benefits of this Grand Division each time of his illness, subject to the foregoing part of this rule. If the Surgeon of the Division sign a certificate for any sick member and thesame be at once left with the Financial Scribe, before 12 o'clock at noon on any day (Sunday excepted), such member shall receiue pay for that day, otherwise it shall not commence until the following day.' Scale 2.—" That all members initiated prior to July 18th, 1883, shall pay under Scale 2, is. per fortnight contributions, to be divided as follows : 10d. to the Benefit Fund, and 2d. to the Management Fund ; and shall be entitled if good upon the books to the following allowance viz. : for the first 26 weeks of such illness,the sum of 10s. weekly •, and should such illness continue, then, for the next 26 weeks the sum of ss. weekly ; and in the event of continued illness, 2s. 6d. per week so long as he remains ill. Should any member who has been in receipt of sick pay declare off the funds of the division, and afterwards declare upon the funds again within the space of 12 calander months, from the time of declaring off, he shall be paid according to such part of the above scale as he was in receipt of when he declared off the funds in the previous illness ; and should any member be afflicted a second time or any number of times, he shall be entitled to receive the full benefits of this Grand Division each time of his illness, subject to the foregoing part of this iule. If the Surgeon of the Division' sign a certificate for any sick member, and the same be at once left with the Financial Scribe, before 12 o'clock at noon on any day (Sunday excepted), such member shall receive pay for that day, otherwise it shall not com- mence until the following day." "That under scale 1, or 2, each member shall be en- titled to £l2 funeral money at his death ; and £lO on the death of his wife, provided such wife has been duly registered to the Funeral Fund, and he hold a certificate of such registration, which certificate must be produced in case of death."_

_ "That rule 25, tables 1, 2,3, 4,5, and 6, (Grand Division Rules), be altered to read six months instead of twelve months. It was decided to hold the next Session at Chester in July next. In the evening a public meeting was held in the-Regent-street Hall, under the presidency of Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, when addresses were delivered by the Rev. J. P. Williams, of Runcorn, and Mr. J. A. Gor- nall, of Chester. Recitations were given by 'Mr. G. Evanson, and Mr. H. Hallmark,of Crewe,Master Moores, and Miss Gaskell of Runcorn, whilst Mr. Thomas Lunt entertained the meeting with an English concertina solo which received a well merited encore. The excellent musical portion of the programme, was in the hands of Mr. Robert Yates and choir. A vote of thanks to the Chairman and entertainers, on the motion of Mr. T. Cooks, seconded by Mr. W. R. Hamilton, of Chester, brought a most pleasant meeting to a close.

div.head: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.

At this court on Thursday, befO-r-e-M-r..-T. H. Gossage and Mr. J. Brock, a summons against the United Alkali Co., for having in their possession, for use in trade twelve weights, which were unjust, was adjourned ' because Inspector Kilpatrick was unable to appear through iilness.—Emma Turner and James Gray were each fined for drunkenness.—Bridget Noon, of Walmsley- street, was bound over to be of good behaviour for three months, for creating a breach of the peace.

div.head: WARRINGTON CONSERVATIVE ASSO-
div.p: WARRINGTON CONSERVATIVE ASSO-

CIA.TION. The annual meeting Of this Association was held at the Conservative Club last night. Mr. R. Pier- point presided, and there were also present Alder- man Sutton, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Councillors Bolton, Muir, Hepherd, Hill; Messrs. J. White, J. Fairclougb, L. W. Reynolds, W. H. Cookson, A. Bennett, &c. There was a good attendance. The report which was of a rosy character was read by Alderman Button, and afterwards adopted, on the motion of Councillor Muir. On the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. John White, a vote of sympathy was passed with the Prince and Princess of Wales and Princess Mary of Peck. A vote of condolence was also passed with the family of the late Mr. E. Whitley, M.P. The bon. treasurer (Mr. J. White), reported that there was a balance of ..£5 2s. 91 due to the treas- urer. The following officers of the Association were elected :—President, Sir G. Greenall ; I hon. sec., Ald. Sutton; hon. treasurer, Mr. John White. A general council was also elected.— Mr. A. Bennett moved a resolution approving of the candidature of Mr. R. Pierpoint. Mr. J. Battersby seconded the resolution, which was carried unani- mously. The Chairman responded, but did not deal with political questions.

div.head: DEATH OF MISS RIGBY AT COLWYN
div.p: DEATH OF MISS RIGBY AT COLWYN
BAY.
FUNERAL AT WARRINGTON.

Miss Rigby, sister of the late Mr. Samuel Rigby, died at her residence, Cclwyn Bay, on Saturday last, in her 80th year, and was interred on Wednesday in We.;rington. A memorial service was previously held in Wycliffe Church, with which the family of the deceased were long and honourably connected when resident in Warrington, and was conducted by the Rev. John Yonge. An address was given by the Rev. Thos. Lloyd, of Colwyn Bay, who made appreciative references to the life and character of the deceased lady as they had come under his observation during her residence at Colwyn Bay for the last eight years. There was a considerable number of relatives and friends of the deceased Mrs.. M. Rigby, Mr. John present, including Rigby, Mr. and Mrs. Z. Armitage, (Altrinc- ham), Mr. and Mrs. R. Armitage, (Grap- penhall), Mr. and Mrs. W. Armitage, jun. Mr. and Mrs. G. F. Armitage, Mr. and Mrs. S. R. Armitage, Mr. and Mrs. Jesse Haworth (Bowdon), Ur. and Mrs. A. H. Lee (Latchford), Mr. W. Ker- shaw (Liverpool), Mr. and Mrs. Simpson (Bowdon), and Mrs. Lloyd (Colwyn Bay). 'be subsequent service at the grave in the cemetery was conducted by the Rev. J. Yonge. Mr. Rigby, the brother of the deceased lady, died in December, 1890, and Mrs. Rigby, his widow, it is sad to record, passed away only a few months afterwards. With the death of Miss Rigby the three members of the family have, therefore, been carried off in little more than a year. - -

- --- In the present time of political stir it will not be Uninteresting to remind our readers i that the late Mr. Rigby was honoured by being invited, n 1868, to become the Liberal candidate for Warrington. He declined to accept the invitation,. contenting himself with working earnestly as chairman of Mr. Peter Rylands's election committee. He continued to be the bead of the Liberal party till 1880, when he was chairman of the election committee of Mr. McMinnies, who, like Mr. Rylands, was elected member for Warrington: The benefactions of Mr. Rigby were very extensive having been computed at a sum not much below £l,OOO a year. He may be said to have been the most munificent supporter of i Dissent n Warrington, and indeed of Wycliffe church he was the mainstay, and contributed about £3060 a year to its support. The severance of an- other important link between Warrington and the past career of the deceased gentleman has taken place in the death of Miss Rigby; add hence the occasion seems a fitting one for recalling some of the chief points in that career.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

JOHN WARRINGTON AGAIN. John Warrington the well-known character of that name, was charged' at the borough police court on Mon- day,with stealing 23. 6d. the property of Mary Lawrenson tripe dealer, &c., Bewsey-St., on Saturday night.—The prisoner had gone into the prosecutrix's shop and asked her to change 6d., which she could not do, but she sent him out to get change for half a crown, and he never came back. Information was given to the polices and be was apprehended by Detecitive Inspector Monaghan, in bed at Daley's lodging-house, and admitted his gat. He was sent to prison for two months with hard labour. ANOTERR MARGARINE PROSECUTION. At the borough police court oil Monday, Catherine Haddock, of 6 Grov,e-street, Latchford, was charged With exposing for sale, on the 18th ult., margarine, without having a label L inches square placed thereon to indicate the nature of the article. Inspector Norman proved the purchase of. a• pound of the article, which was unlabelled, and the public analyst eertifying it to be margarine., She pleaded ignorance.—The Chairman said the Bench were disposed to view the matter leni- ently under the circumstances, though they would perhaps expose themselves to criticism for doing so. She would be fined 10s. including costs. CRUELTY Td A HORSE.—A. STRANGE REMEDY Fon SrLyIN. - • • At the Warrington County Sessions, on Wednesday, Henry Critchlev was charged with cruelly ill-treating al • horse, at Poulton, on the 2nd inst.—P.S: Barnes deposed' . that he was passing alone Warrington-road; at Poulton, about 11 p.m. on the 2nd inst., when he heard a hcirse in a field making a frightful noise. •He went into the field and found the horse "all in a heap," with Its back up, trembling violently, and apparently starved. There was not a particle of food near it, and the ground was covered with 2 incties.of snow, and the animal had no, shelter. He sent P.C. Pope to :ascertain to whom the horse belonged, and he returned with the defendant, who said the horse was suffering from rheumatism and he had been advised by Mr. Bennett's man that leaving , it out all night would cure it. Witness told him that was the hest thing to kill it.—The Chairman (Major Pickmere) : A strange remedy. —lnspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., gave conjirmatory evidence. He ad- , rnittO ,that Mr. Comber and Mr. Bennett also had horses but all the same night, but said they had a shed to go to and plenty of hay.—The defendant said he told the sergeant that the horse was suffering from spavin ; and he was advised to keep it out all night as a cure, a thing which was commonly done. He fed the horse , three times thap day. ,He called John Ratford on his behalf, who said the horse was turned out on the 17th of Nov. night and day, but could not speak as to the 2nd inst. He would not have turned his own horse out such a night.—Defendant`-said he had had the horse killed after hearing of the prosecution.—He was fined 10s. and costs. CLAIM BY MASTER TANNERS AGAINST A WORKMAN. At the Borough Magistrates" Court, yesterday, the executors of the late S. Reynold% tanners, of Latchford, clairnud from Henry Connor the sum of LI. for neglect of work. Mr. Browne appeared. for the prosecution. The defendant, be said, gave on, Monday, the 11th inst., a week's toptice to leave. He Worked only from 9 a.m. until 2.3o.that day, from 6 a.ln. till 10 a.rn. on the Tues- • day, on Use Wednesday not at all, and on the Thursday, he started at 9 a.m. and worked until Saturday. The defendant was one of a -gang te the head of which the wages were:paid,and he divided the money. Through the absence from work of Connor and others the plaintiffs had suffered a loss of about £2O, but they only asked for nominal damages, by way of example. Another man had been summoned, but he paid, and the ease was withdramn.—Mr. Hartley, manager for the plaintiffs, supported this statement, and the. Bench gave a deci- sion against the defendant, who did not appear, for pay- ment of the amount claitned. ' CLAIM FOR WAGES AGAINST MESSRS. CROSFIED.—Drs. I,IISSAL OF ,MEN WITEOUT NOTICE, , At the Borough Police Court yesterday, before Mr. Jahn White (chairman), .and Aldermen Harrison and Wright, George Henry Walker, 50,, Burchall-st., sum- moned Messrs. John Crostlehd and Sons, Bank Quay, for recovery of 18s. a week's wages, alleged to be due in lieu of a week's notice. He said that three weeks be- fore Christmas he went and asked the defendant's man- ager for a job, and he was started as -a labourer,nothing being mentioned about either wages or notice. He was paid 18s. a week, and on the 19th inst., he was paid off wsthout notice. He said he claimed a'week's noticeibut. the reply was "I don't know about that : that is not re- quired." Witness said "Some one will have to know." Be saw Dr. Malcolm, and he said he could not find any- thing fOr him to do. Witness asked him about a week's , notice, and he said he knew nothing about it. Theig were notices posted up by the firm that any man leaving the firm's employ must give a week's notice, and he thought, that being the case, he was entitled to a week's notice.— A representative of the firm attended and stated thatwhat the plaintiff said was true, but the man was employed as a casual labourer.—Alderman Harrison: What do yod mean by a casual labourer? A man can't surely be discharged at a moment's notice.—The representa- tive of the firm : Oh Yes.—Alderman Harrison : Why, surely that is hardly fair.—ln reply to Alderman Harrison it was stated that plaintiff was only dealt with as casual labourers usually were, but no conditions were men- tioned when he was engaged.—Alderman Harrison said in that case he came' as an ordinary workman.—The Chairman read a notice handed up to him, which stated that no man w ould be discharged without receiving a week's notice or a week's pay instead, unless for drunk- - enness, disorderly conduct, or neglect of work, in which , case he would be dismissed; and asked if the plaintiff had been guilty of any of these things.—Messrs. Cros- field's representative : No, the only fault we had to find leas laziness and incapacity to work, and instructions were given me to dismiss him.—Alderman Harrison asked if the plaintiff declined to do any work, and was in- formed that he did not; he was only slow. He told the plaintiff he was not entitled to a week's notice as he had only `been employed four weeks.—The Chairman said the notice said every man was entitled, and mentioned nothing about four weeks.—The Bench decided in fav- our of the plaintiff.

MR. JOHN REDMOND'S HUNDRED- GUINEA WATCH. In connection with the robbery of a hundred-guinea presentation watch from Mr. John Redmond, M.P., at a Dublin railway station on Saturday night, the Dublin detectives made a clever capture on Monday night. actlng on information Detective-officers Tuohy and Montgomery proceeded to the Liverpool boat and ar- rested two men, who gave the names of Flynn and Jones, as they were about to sail for England. The case of the watch was found in the pocket of one of them broken into small pieces, while on the other was found a gold chain, which was stolen from one of the visitors to Mr. Paynell's grave at Glasnevin on Sunday. One of the prisoners on being arrested attempted to assault the officer, but was immediately overpowered, and both were locked up.

V Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY. WARRINGTON v. MANCHESTER RANGERS.

Contrary to expectation, this match was played at Rusholnse, on Saturday, The heavy fall of snow was followed by a severe frost on Friday evening, but the Rangers evidently bent on having a match at whatever cost, had the ground cleared, The turf vias in capital I condition, but along the popular side especially the snow was in such large quantities that it rendered accurate play an impossibility. Several of the -Warringtonians,. assuming that there would be no match, failed to put in an appearance, but, luckily, the second reserve were at hand, their match with Birkenhead St. Ann's having I been cancelled. A combination having been secured,' the prospects of maintaining the record of having beaten the Rangers on their native heath were indeed remote, with an absence of six first team, especially when it was found that the Manchester club had whipped together their strongest fifteen. The weather was bitterly cold, and there would not be more than 250 persons present when Turner kicked off in the teeth of a strong east wind. A quarter of an hour each way sufficed for the afternoon's sport. Warburton, Donohue and John T. Bate foiled the return, and the oval was at once taken to the Rangers' quarters. The first to show up was James Bate, who tricked Parlane finely, and raced to Cunliffe, and passing finely at the right moment„ the chance was as badly mulled. This mis- take led up to Boscow's charge being attacked, but the Warrington custodian, assisted by Evans, was not found wanting, and the goal escaped disaster. Potts accounted for H. Hasleham in fine style on one occasion, and a pass from Parlane to Pollard was badly mulled. This acted as relief, for Turner, Berry, and Ashton, after rushing the leather beyond the half-way flag, found their efforts seconded, by Heesom, Evans, and James Bate, the Rangers' 25 flag being reached. Scrimmages succeeded each other along the popular side, until at last a fair catch by the Rangers enabled Turner to relieve a threatening, attack of the opposing forwards. Potts essayed to get through , without suc- cess, and then a kick being awarded the Rangers by way of penalty, a shot at goal was taken, a minor beity,'' re- corded. This was the only point scored during this half, land no time was lost in turniug found; the cold, if any- thing, being more severe than at the opening of hostili- ties. The Warringtonians made direct for the home lines on the kick off, and Boscow, by a long kick in the first minute, registered a minor. Some brilliant play by the Bates, Berry, Heesom, and Evans found the latter run- ning in touch a yard from the line, certainly hard lines for Warrington, after the only bit of decent play seen during the afternoon. Cunliffe saved again fro:n a rush, and some smart paising initiated by Donohue found Turner kicking well, the Rangers again conced- ing a minor. A clevef 'tackle of Bogg by Heesom en- dangered the home goal, but the extra yard could not be gained, and although Bate got away on one occasion, and looked all over a scorer, the tackling was safe, and the end came as a relief to both players and spectators, with the result as a draw, Warrington having four minors to the Rangers' two. Teams :—Warrington Bosqow, back; Potts, Heesom, and Evans, three-quarter backs; J. T. Bate and John Bate, half backs; Ashton. Berry, Teare, Fair. Turner, Donohue, Molyneaux Ed- wards, Warburton, and Foster, forwards. Manchester Rangers: A. E. Cunliffe, back ; W. G. Sabin (captain), G. Pollard, and M. Begg, three-quarter backs; Parlane and Entwistle, half backs; Robert Hasleham, Herbert Hasleham,•ll. Ashton, T. Westbrook, T. Comman, W. Pearson, L. Haslam, Jones, and R. Hammett, forwards. RUNCORN v: NEW BRIGHTON. The severe weather of last week interfered with this match, which was set down for decision at the Irwell- lane ground. Despite the fact that precautions had been taken to preserve the ground, it was not found necessary to remove the hay. An .exhibition match was indulged in, and Runcorn won by three goals and two tries to nil. Crompton was in fine form, - crossing the line on three occasions. Of course the match counts as a draw. WIDNES v, TUEBROOK. The above teams met on Saturday on the Widnes ground, and after the captains of the teams had con- sulted together for some time on the condition of the around, it was decided to play an " exhibition "game. Result—Widnes, 4 tries, (8 points) ; Tuebrook, 1 goal, 1 try, (7 points).

GREAT LOSS OF LIFE. TIFLIS, MONDAY.—The religious ceremony of blessing the waters, performed here to-day, was attended by a terrible disaster. The procession had left the Armenian Cathedral, and, followed by a dense throng of,pepple,was passing over a temporary bridge erected over an arm of .the river liura, when the structure suddenly collapsed. Atinass of people fell with the bridge into the stream. Others struggled to force their way back from the broken badge on to the land, but were met by the surging crowd presSin.g forward. Many were crushed to death or in= jured in thepress, while many more were drowned in the river. The greatest consternation prevailed, and it Is Impossible as yet to ascertain the number of victims.

away it would be better for all of them. As to other departments of the Corporation Alderman Sutton would - tell them about these, and Mr. Morris would speak with respect to the town and trade of Warrington, as to the best paying part of it. With regard to the law he could not say that was in_a flourishing condition at present (Laughter.) Mr. Forshaw would tell them that in the saw things were very low, but they were risinfr. He was sure both he and his partner looked flourishing • their corporations improved. (Laughter.) He coupled the toast with the names of Alderman Sutton and Mr. Thomas Morris. .

Alderman Strrros etpressed his regret that the Mayor was not present to respond, and the hope that he would soon regain his health, and be able to resume his mayoral duties. (Applause.) He had nodoubt the Cor- poration had done their best, and all they could for the benefit of the town, but it would have been better if they had done more in the shape of improvements. He ' was el opinion that during the last 15 to 18 years—and that included the time he himself had been a member I —they had done more in that way than ever before. (Much laughter and applause.) They had acquired by purchase the gas works, for which they were principally indebted to the chairman, and they had turned out a financial success. (Applause.) They' had obtained for the borough that grand Town Hall, and the gardens for the public, in which acquisition again their friend, Mr. Davies, was instrumental in bringing about. (Ap- plause.) They had more recently acquired the water works—(renewed applause)—and he wished their prede- cessors had purchased them at an earlier period. If they had done so they would have got them at a com- paratively low price, and they would now have been tree from debt. The Corporation had widened a portion of Bridge-st., and there was looking them in the face a very important improvement which would soon or late have to be attended to, the widening of the other por- tion of Bridge-st. That would cost a very large sum, and he only regretted, that their predecessors had not the foresight to purchase as much of the property in Bridge-st. as was necessary for, the purpose, for if they had they would have got it for a much smaller sum than would have tn be paid in the tame.

- - Mr. MO i BRIS n responding remarked that if Mr. Carleton (who had now taken his departure) had treated his subject ecclesiastically instead of politically, he would have deserved more credit. So far as the trade of the town was concerned the iron trade by which he got his bread and cheese flumuated from prosperity-to adversity so often that he hardly dare say how it was, If he said it was very good it would go before the Conciliation Board of South Staffordshirer'and the ironworkers would want an advance in wages.. (Laughter.) If he said it was bad the ironmasters would say there must be a re- duction of wages. (Laughter.) But it was going on 'fairly well : there was nothing to boast about on either side. The men employed were getting decent wages with which he thought they were well satisfied ; he wished they were always so satisfied. But there was that contemptible Tariff Bill called M‘Kinley's Tariff; which had affected the whole of England more or less. In 1890 there were over 26,000 tons of hoop iron sent from Eng- land to the United States, whereas in 1891 through this M`Kinley Bill . only 500 tons were sent. Supposing the ironmasters got or 116 a ton for this iron, that meant that £130,000 was taken from the workmen and capital'of this country, and the district that , sustained this loss was Warrington and a radius of 30 miles round. If it suffered as mach what must be the distress caused throughout the whole country by this M'Kinley Tariff Bill? Whether the money would do as much, good where it had gone as it had, done us he doubted as most of it went into the pockets of the manufacturers in America. It was like coining money for them. They could afford to buy up representatives in the senatl. They could send £l,OOO to a man to vote a certain way when they knew they would make £2,000 by it. He hoped the 'day would never come in England when our representatives would be bought and sold. (Applause.) He believed if we could send over some straightforward fellows to sit in the House of Representatives 'at Washington, who would leaven the whole lump into a sort of righteous- ness' we should live in England in clover as we never did before. But as long as old England kept up the quality and finish of its manufacture, and neat packing to mak* goods look well, she would never lose the day, if there were a thousand M'Kinleys. The proceedings were enlivened with performances on the trombone, cornet, and piano by Messrs. Anderton, Thos. Litine, and In. Rose. We may mention that in the course of the evening a

telegram of condolence on the death of the Dula of Clarence was despatched from the society, by the Chair- man, to the Prince and Princess of Wales. A reply was received, on Tuesday night, from Sandringham, as follows :—" Davies, Blue Coat Brotherly Society, War- ringtOn : Thank you for deep sympathy.—EQUEßßY."

PRESENTATION TO THE LATE LATCH- FORD STATIONMASTER. On Saturday evening at the residence of the Mayor (Alderman Greenell), at Hill Top, Latchford, a ptesentation was made to Mr. Joseph Harrison, late stationmaster at Latehford, and recently appointed night stationmaster at Lime-street sta- 'tion, Liverpool. The committee who have had the matter in hand are Mr. Wm. Nerpoint, the execu- tors of S. Reynolds, Mr. W. Tinsley, Messrs. Parkinson and Co., Messrs. P. Davies, and IL Roberts ioint secretaries, and the Mayor treasurer. The Mayor presided, and Messrs. P: Davies, and H. Roberts were also present. Mr_ DAVIES read a letter he had received a letter from Mr. W. Pierpoint stating his inability to attend through illness, but expressing himself as glad that the efforts on Mr. Harrison's bebalf had had such a good result. Mr. Davies observed that Mr. Harrison might take it from him that the collection of subscriptions had not been an arduous duty. He had had no trouble in inducinz people to subscribe, and it had been a very great plea— sure indeed to him to undertake the task. Mr. Davies then read the address, which was signed by himself and co-secretary and the Mayor on behalf of the inhabitants of Latchford and neighbourhood, and which has already been published in our colueens. Mr. ROBERTS having congratulated the Mayor on being so far restored to health as to be able to take part in the. present interesting and agreeable ceremony, observed that his own share in the matter had been extremely. small ; Mr. Davies and the Mayor deserved by far the greater amount of credit. The object of the presenta- tion was to show the estimation in which he was held for his courtesy and kindness as master of Latchford station; and his personal worth of character by which he had se impressed the people of the neighbour- hood generally that there had been no difficulty in ob- taining' from them their expression of this. He hoped that Mr. Harrison in the important position he now held would feel that his past conduct was in a great measure the cause of his being where he was that day, and that it would encourage him to be determined that the same principles of conduct should continue to actuate him in the future, so that he might rise to a stilt higher and better position in the service of the Company employ- ing him for which he was sure he had the ambition, and he believed, the ability. Mr. Roberts concluded by wish- ing Mrs. Harrison better health and even greater success to Mr. Harrison in the future„ assuring him of the good wishes of all he represented. The MAYOR then said on behalf of the subscribers and the joint seeretaries he had now much pleasure in handing to Mr. Harrison the illuminated address and a purse containing 40 guineas, subscribed for by the -inhabitants of Latchford and neighbourhood in recogni- tion of Mr. Harrison's conduct as station-master at Latchford. The secretaries would bear him out when he said that the proposal to thus show their appreciation of him had been well received on all sides. No pressure had been put upon anyone in bringing the matter for- ward; and the response to the appeal had been prompted purely by friendship, and good feeling towards Mr. [ Harrison, on account of his courtsey and kindness. He hoped the money would be of service to him and help i him in bettering his condition in the future, that the ' address would remind him of some old faces in years to come, and that they might see him some day in a yet higher position than at present. Mr. HARRISON said he scarcely knew how to express himself in thanking them for that beautiful address and the purse that he now held in his hand. As to his con- ,duct in the past he had tried to do his duty to all classes who had used the trains at Latchford. He had been I sent specially to Latchford station to see if he could im- prove matters there. It was formerly a poor little place, but it had been re-done up, and as you might say, re- built, and there had now been there for years one of the I most convenient stations on the line. In connection with the goods traffic there had only been room for 13 wagons; now there was room for 50. There was batter accommodation there now than ever there hacrbeen be- fore, and he felt that he had tried to carry out the wishes of Mr. Shaw and Mr. Braie in this matter of improving the station. He had bOn in the employ of the Company for over 20 years, and he felt that it was owing to his exertions at Latchford that he had gained [ the responsible position he now occupied; and he was determined, if possible, to climb the ladder still higher. He should always prize the address they had presented to him, and when he saw it, he would, as the Mayor had said, think of their faces; and be should point his boys to it,. and try to stimulate them to [do their duty in whatever sphere they might be placed. [ He thanked Mr. Roberts for the mention of his wife. Be hoped she would have better health in Liverpool than she had had at Latchford. Owing to the change she had not been well up to the present, but he thought from what medical men told him, that she would im- prove. 'On the motion of Mr. ROBERTS, seconded by Mr. P. DAVIES, a vote of thanks was accorded to the Mayor for presiding, Mr. Roberts remarking that the matter had been brought to such s. success largely through the Mayor having consented to act as treasurer of the fund.

George Beckett, aged twenty-one, was on Tuesday remanded by the Shrewsbury magistrates on a charge of stealing a watch, a watch chain, a sovereign, and cer- tain articles of clothing, belonging to his employer, Thomas Buckley, bailiff, Grimshall, Salop. It was stated that the prisoner bad eloped with the prosecu- tor's wife.

WA ItRINGTON CONSERVATIVE WARD MEETINGS. ORFORD WARD. A meeting of Conservatives of Orford Ward was held on Monday evening in Rennet-street school- room. Leintenant-Colonel Bolton presided, and Mr. R. Pierpoint, the Conservative candidate, was present during part of the evening. The following ward officers were elected :—Chairman, Leiutenant- Colonel Bolton ; vice-chairman. Messrs. Grounds and W. H. J. Jenkins;. secretary, Mr. P. Edgar. Mr. Edgar, in the course of a few remarks, said he was beginning to think that Orford Ward was one
of the " blael spots" of Radicalism, although Mr. Hampson assured him that, by proper working, the ward could be won by the Conservatives. The CHAIRMAN remarked that Mr. R.Pierpoint was a . .

native of the town, and surely they were not going to be led to believe that the good old town of Warrington had to send across the Channel to Dublin for a repre- sentative in the House of Commons. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Pierpoint had the interests of the workingman at heart, he knew the ins and outs of the commercial system of the whole country,and had travelled far and wide,and therefore he (the Chairman). considered it would be a standing disgrace to " the town if they had to find a stranger to represent them in the House of Commons. (Hear, hear.) Mr. R. PrERPOINT, who was well received, said that at a meeting which took place a few days ago some of their opponents were good enough to devote a certain amount of time to him, and to what he had said. He was happy to say that what they had said about him took the part of a little good-humoured chaff about which he had nothing whatever to complain. But his opponent, Dr. Houston, asked him a few questions He wanted to know why Lord Salisbury did not previously tell the country the details of the Coercion Act he passed after begot into power in 1886. He would, however", remind Dr. Houston that in the beginning of 1888 when the Conservative Government was for a short time in power the Chancellor of the Exchequer gave notice, on be- half of his right honourable friend the Secretary for Ireland, that a Bill would be introduced' for the suppres- sion of the Land Leave. When the Unionists again came into office later on in the year with a powerful majority an attempt WeS,made for some time to govern Ireland without any exceptional powers but it was found that this was impossible. The Act that was passed was far less stringent than Mr.. Gladstones for under it Irishmen had slaver been put in prison without trial. (Hear, hear.) Dr. Houston had also asked why Lord Salisbury did not say .what be was going to put in the Land Purchase Act,, but he would remind them that that Act was only an extension of what had gone before and did not involve any constitutional change. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Pierpoint then alluded at some-length-to Home Rule and to.the British occupation of Egypt. _ On the motion of Mr. PETER WELLS, seconded by Mr. Horot4 a resolution approving of Mr.. Plerpoint's candi- ture was carried. 'A. vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meetina _

SOCIETY. ANNUAL DINNER.

Rugby players were not only "unemployed "on Saturday. Play was not possible in some of the Associ- ation matches, whilst several of the most important of the F.A. Cup ties were postponed. This was the case at Sheffield, Evertor'' Preston, and Sunderland kelbion v. Birmingham t. George's). At each of these four places the afternoon was filled up by exhibitions only, so that the football that took place does not call for comment. Even in some instances where the tie was presumably brought off protests were lodged, and it is, quite probable that a good many of the games will be replayed on Saturday next, other dates btlng found for the disturbed fixtures.

When the Blackburn Rovers had the worst of their League encounter with Derby County a fortnight ago they were poorly represented. Both their full backs, Forbes and M'Keown, were away. These trusty men were in their places in the tie on Saturday, and the re- sult was that the cupholders won by four to one. They, gave a pretty fair sample of their cup form, although they are still without Barton, one of their half-backs. Southworth benefitted by his brief .rest and scored all the goals. The Rovers have unearthed a Useful right • wing player in Haydock,of tbe reserve, and it is scarcely likely that Lofthouse will be wanted again when his suspension expires. J. Goodall was not at his best, and , the forward department of. the visitors left a•good deal to be desired, whilst Robinson has frequently kept goal I better.

The loss of Oswald s services quite spoiled the chances of Notts at Sunderland, and they were easily vanquished., The beaten side took the precaution of protesting despite the liberal layer of sand. This game was .wittlessed by the biggest gathering of the afternoon, something like 15,000 persons being present. Woverhampton Wanderers were expected to make short work of Crewe Alexandra. They were not equal to it, however' and although an extra half-back was occupied each team was credited with a couple of goals This will necessitate the Wolves visiting Crewe. The advantage of ground was supposed to turn the tide in favour of Bootle' but to theit astonish- ment Darwen not only overplayed but beat them by two goals to nil. This is the best thing Darwen have accom- plished for many weeks.

Bolton Wanderers were the only League team to suffer a reverse during the afternoon, but as this was only a kind of practice game they will have a chance of doing better when the tie is actually played. There was a capital attendance, the crowd numbering upwards of 12,000.

Rugby fixtures clntinue to be sadly disarranged owing to the severity of the weather. If this state of affairs goes on much longer players will get out of form and misleading results may be looked for. The list of abandoned matches was very large on Saturday, and it was only where grounds had been thoroughly well pro- tected that football was even attempted.

The Yorkshiremen are counting upon the Rugby championship as a practical certainty, and they are probably not far out in their reckoning. Their matches against Somersetshire and Devonshire not only yielded easy victories but served to strengthtin their play generally, and they seam to think they have now the best team it is possible to bring together out of the manv-acred shire. The centre three-quarters position is still admitted to be a weak spot, as Sumersgill.lacks the necessary experience. No one has ye been found to adequately fill the void created by the suspensibn of Sutcliffe. Yorksliire expect to meet Kent next Monday, and the Midland Counties a weak later, and they are pretty confident about coming through both safely.

-- Little interest was shown in the meeting of the Man- chester Rangers and Warrington at Rusholme, where, owing to the time expended in removing the snow, the start was delayed for an hour. Even when a beginning was made both the teams were weak. They were pretty well matched, however, so much so that not a point was obtained throughout the match. -

The 37th annual dinner of the Warrington .Blue Coat Brotherly Society was held in the Assembly Room of the Conservative Club on Monday evening. Mt. Stanley Higham, manager of the club, was the caterer, and a most excellent repast, promptly and' admirably served up, was provided. Mr. Joseph Davies, president of the Society,occupied the chair, and Mr. Edward Rose, master of the Blue Coat

School, the vice-chair. There were also- pre- sent by the Rev. E. U. E. Carleton, vicar of Holy Trinity church, Aldermen Wright and Sutton, Councillor James Fairclough; Mr. P. Davies, Dr. C. White Mr. Tfiomas Morris, Mr. Frederick Monks, Mr. V. J. Forshaw, secretary of the Society, Mr. W. Owen, Mr. Charles Twiss, and Mr. E. Aukland. The Casiraux after expressing pleasure at seeing scr many present and regret at the hiability of Major Pick- mere, Mr. J. C. Parr, and Mr. Merchant to attend, pro- posed the first toast,the health other Majesty the Queen. He remarked that he could Understand the compaby receiving that toast with silence because she was Net now passing through a heavy cloud, and they only hoped she might be sustained by the providence of God Al- mighty in the trouble she was at present called upon to bear. They knee that her deceased grandson was a special favourite of the Queen, and they were sure that she must feel his death extremely. He the Chairman) must ask them to drink with great sympathy her health. By way of showing their deep regret and sympathy for her Majesty, there would be no songs sung that night. (Hear, hear.) Might God preserve and sustain her in her great calamity. The toast wasilhen drunk, the National Anthem being
sung by the company, The CaAmu/4 then proposed the toast of the Prince and Princess of Wales, remarking that, at that time last week they should have coupled it with the Duke of

Clarence, now no more. Mr. W. OWEN proposed the toast of the bishop and clergy of the diocese and ministers of all denominations, coupled with the name of the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton. He remarked that he was sorry to say that owing to the health of the bishop they saw very little of him, but he heard from a clergyman that night, that he was better, and that probably they would see more of him in future. The clergy of the Church af England in the town, he was sure, were doing their duty as well as they could. Though a churchman by training and conviction he still had the very heartiest and sincerest sympathy with the ministers of all other denominations ; and he believed , the sympathy of those present was as great as his. If he were asked what the difficulty was with which the clergy and Ministers of all other denominations had to grapple with he should say it was the great, and grdw- ing indifference to the services of the churches and chapels. This appeared to him to be the fact both from the censuses taken for,certain purposes and from what he had seen ; and be left the solution of this question to his friend Mr. Carleton. The Rev. E. C. E. Cararrox, in responding, said he had great pleasure in doing so, not only on behalf of the Church of England, but also on behalf of the other denominations, because he thought the good feeling that existed amongst all classes of the Church in Warrington was generally acknowledged. Re thought that good feeling would be very likely even to survive the General Election, if only their political friends would leave them alone, but he was afraid, judging from some utterances he had seen in the papers, from a distinguished visitor, that there was a disposition on the part of some to have them turned out of the Church. If that was so, he thought he was justified in saying, that as they knew whence the provocation proceeded, they would have the sympathy of theMpeeple in making it hot for the indivi- dual who came so far to set them by the ears. It was all very well to say that the attack was only going to be made upon the Church of Wales. That meant an attack upon the Church of England, inasmuch as the former was a part of the latter : there was no episcopal church in Wales, any more than in Lancashire or Cheshire,sepa- rate from the Church of England. There were at pre- sent English parishes, some in Shropshire, for instance, which lay in the Welsh diocese of St. Asaph, and there were Welsh parishes that lay in the English diocese of Hereford. Those who said they were going to attack the Church in Wales, not in England, were like the man who said he was not going to rob the house, , but only going to strip the drawing room. The ground for attacking the church in Wales was that it was Weak. He was afraid that Wales was not the only place where the church was weak—though it had been growing stronger for some time. He should like some of their Nonconformist friends to consider how they would like to be served with the same sauce—to have people going about, visiting their places of worship, and taking stock of their congregations,then coming to them and saying" Well, lam very sorry, but you are not in as flourishing a condition as you might be ; you are really not strong; wouldn't it be better for usto take a little of the property you have got together, and use it for purposes of public utility ?" He supposed for pay- ing members of Parliament for instance. The gentleman he referred to did not, he thought, object to endowments even to those that came out of the pockets of the tax- paper, and he (Mr. Carleton) thought they would pre- fer to endow religion rather than to endow politicans. The same feeling that led pious people in times past to endow churches led them also to endow institu- tions like the Warrington Blue Coat School, and he thought they would agree with him that they had all a common interest in preserving those trusts from un- righteous invasion. (Applause.) Mr. Frederick MONIS proosed the toast of " The army, navy, and volunteers." Re said he was a mem- ber of the Peace Sciciety,but could nevertheless heartily propose that toast, because he was satisfied that the best way to preserve peace was to be always prepared for lwar. Depend upon it when the time came that we dis- ' banded our army,, destroyed our navy, and reduced our volunteer force to a mere police body, then the time of kEngland's decay would begin. He coupled with the r toast the name of Dr. White. Dr. WHITE, who was formerly in the militia, responded at some length. The doctor then pro- posed the toast of the evening "The Warring- ton Blue Coat Brctherly Society." He said he did not know how this valuable society began. It might have been copied from a similar institution in another town, or it might have been an emanation from the prolific brain of their chairman, or the production of the late Mr. Bowes. He rather thought the gentleman he had last mentioned had the honour of parentage. However it might be, they might be assured that the institution was a genuine Anglo-Saxon one, and sprang from no theoretical need, but from a practical necessity. The doctor pointed the 'Blue Coat boys present, to the Chair- man and others there as examples of men who had been Blue Coat boys, and by persevering effort had risen to high position in the town—gentlemen, who he said, had had the highest municipal honours thrust upon them, though he did not mean to say that every lad at that table would be a mayor. He was very much charmed to see on a cottage that Mr. Monks was build- ing an inscription, which was something to this effect— From labour you gain honour, by. well-,doing you gain happiness, by frugality you gain independence. There was a sound truth and philosophy in this, and if the boys of the school would keep steadily before them this standard of principle they would make advancement. It had occurred to him that it might be possible to take some house, at which the boys after they left school might be accommodated, where circumstances necessi- tated it, and have beds and their meals, and meet together. As one of the trustees he should be very glad to aid any effort in the direction, not only of making such provision, but also of providing for unfortunate members. He coupled with the toast the name of Mr. Forshew. Mr.' W, J. Fonstcaw read letters from Mr. Ti. Greenall. and Alderman Harrison regretting their inability to be present ; the former desiring to be put down-as a Sub- scriber of a guinea. Mr. Forshaw then read the annual report of the Society. Their proceedings, this year, it stated, had been in every viay, satisfactory. The sub- scriptions during the past year had been £29 19s, ed., and £44 12s. 10d. had been expended in assistance of members. The Society had now a balance at the bank of £33 19s. 81.. The society had introduced a new feature, that of offering monetary assistance to sisterly Blues who had continued in their situations for 12 months and had good characters. The report deplored the death of Major Litton, a generous subscriber to the society's funds, and for many years a valuable trustee of the school. Mr. Forshaw then, responding to the toast just proposed, said the society was, as the report ' showed, in a fairly prosperous condition ; and he hoped it would continue to be so. The Committee took a very warm interest in their work, and endeavoured to carry out the objects, and to dispense the funds, in accordance with the wishes of the members. Some years ago the notion of a Home was propounded by Mr. Monks, and,, endeavours were made to get sufficient funds to erect one, but after the death of Air. Bowes, who was then president of the society and one of the founder a with Mr. Davies, the matter fell through. The Vica-Cnatmkri proposed the toast of" The trus- tees of the Blue Coat School," and read a telegram from Mr. W. S. Burgess regretting his inability to be present to propose this toast. Mr. W. Poem% briefly supported the toast. The Onataman, who rose amidst hearty applause, responded. He said it bad always been a pleasant duty for him to go to the school and see that it was pro- perly administered. Mr. Percy Divp.s, in the absence of Mr. Parr, pro- posed in a humorous speech, the toast of" The Mayor. and Corporation and the tOwn and trade of Warrington." The Mayor, he said, they would agree with him, did his best, and was doing very- Well, and he hoped he would have better health than in the past year, in which case lie was sure he would continue to do well. Of course we were not all oraters;and he Might not speak very well, but he would do his best. As to the Corporation' some parte of it he very much admired ; other parts he did not admire at all. The gas was very bad, and had gone down that flight, aed the Corporation accordingly went down in their estirnation for the momeat. He was not going into nasty particulars about the intercepting depots, but , they were a nuisance, and if they were a little further : q, I

The meeting for Howlet. Ward was held on Tuesday evening, in the National schools Church-st. Mr. John Fairclough presided, and amongst those on the platform were Mr. R. Pierpoint, the Conservative candidate, Councillors Bolton and Cannell, Messrs. A. Bennett, W. Diggle, Mason and Dewhurst. There was a good attend- ance. The following Ward officers were elected : Chair- man, Mr. John Fairclough ; vice-chairman, Councillor Bolton Dr. Cannell, and Mr. J. V. Taylor ; hon. secret- ary, dr. T. Mason.

Mr. R. riERPOIXT, who was well received, congratu- lated the Conservative electors of the ward on the vic- tory they had achieved at the last municipal elections, and 'also upon the candidate they had returned. He had taken upon himself some few days ago to criticise what his opponents had said, or rather had not said, concerning Horne Rule. He knew- they all wished to be rid of Home Rule, and rid of it for ever, but they must remember that the next general election would mainly turn upon that great question. In England Protestants and Roman Chtliolics could live happily together with- out disliking each other, but if they read this history of Ireland they found a very different state of things they found that, in the past,the utmost hatred prevailed between the two religious bodies, and they found also that, when Home Rule was proposed, the erotestants Ulster were wholly opposed to it. They must not forget that Ulster was the most prosperous and the most in- dustrious part of Ireland. Were they in England, who were mainly Protestants, going to hand over their Protestant brethren in Ulster to the tender • mercies of the Roman Catholics of Ireland(" No, no,!' and "Never.") That was a thing very seriously to be considered, and he hoped that not only the Protestants of the Church of England but also the Protestants of other denominations would take it into very serious consideration. The Pro- testantsof Ulster were citing to the Protestants of Eng- land to come over and help them. Should the Home Rule Bill be passed and Ulster included in it there was •an imminent danger of civil war. (Hear, hear.) His • opponent said, however, that Ulster was to be included in the Home Rule Bill, but would they allow that ? ("No.") Let them include Ulster in the Bill and then he apprehended the electors of this country would say that they would have no such Bill. (Applause.) His opponent had toucned upon another matter, and that was the appointment of Irish judges and he said the judges would be appointed by the Mil executive with the exception of the judges of the Irish Exchequer Court. He (Mr. Pierpoint) looked forward to such a thing with the greatest apprehension. An Irish exe- cutive must, to a large extent, be composed of the present Home Rule members of Parliament, and who were the men who would have a prior claim to be appointed judges ? He supposed there were no men who would have so Strong a claim to seats on the bench as Mr. Timothy Healy, the hero of the horse-whipping, and Mr. Harrington. (Laughter.) He asked them whether a court presided over in Ulster by Mr. Timothy Healy or Mr. Harrington would be likely to have the respect of the community. (Laughter.) It was also proposed that the police should be appointed by the Irish executive, but he thought that, when they con- , sidered the scenes that had lately gone on in Ireland, they would see that the police were very much better in the hands of the imperial government. (Hear, hear.) Alluding to the question of one man one vote Mr. Pier point said he was net prepared to argue, nor was he ab- solutely, against, the system, but if they were again going to put the electoral power of this country again in the furnace they must do it pretty thoroughly and not simply take one little matter. There was one important matter, and that was the over-representation of Ireland. (Hear, bear ) He did not see why Ireland should have a larger proportionate representation than England or Scotland, and yet, Ireland had now, according to popu- lation, Some 13 to 18 more members than it had a right to have. If ir were determined to have a change in the system of representation in England he asked them to insist on Englishmen and Scotchmen having a proper proportion of representation. (Applause.) Mr. Pier- point also declared himself against disestablishrnent,and in favourof compensation to publicans in case of taking from him by legislation what lie was either legally, or, according to old-fashioned morality, supposed to be the owner of. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Dr. Cannell moved a resolution approving of the can- didature of Mr. Pierpoint. This., was secokded by Mr. Diggle, supported by Cduncillor Bolton, and Mr. A. Bennett, and carried. A vote of thanki to the Chair- man concluded the meeting. • FAIRFIELD WARD. A meeting of Conservatives of Fairfield Ward was held on Wednesday evening in the Pariah Church Mission Room, Brick-st. Alderman Francomb presided, and amongst those present en the platform wereere Captain Buckton, Mr. W. Gill, as well as the candidate, Mr. R. Pierpoint. The CHAIRMAN in a few opening referred to the burial of the Duke of Clarence, and said that he supposed there had been that day more genuine sorrow and more genuine tears in the country than perhaps in the memory of any one of them. ' They must all have been struck with the loyalty shown by the people of Warrington that day. Those who could spare the time paid a visit to the Parish Church, and others closed their shops. It had not been a matter purely of Conservatives or Church people or any particular sect; everybody joined in .showing whatever respect they could to the memory of the de- parted Prince. (Rear, hear.)

- THE LICENSING LAWS AND ALTERATIONS
TO PREMISES.

Sir,—l note in your issue of Saturday last a report in connection with the alterations at the "Lion Hotel," re the opening of a door in Ship-yard. May I ask, has the sanction and approval of the Licensing Magistrates been panted, and, if so, was any notification given by the applicants, for what I consider a new license ? If nil, memory fails me, have not two licenses during the past thirty years in the said " Ship-yard " ceased to exist,owing to the class of people that then frequented? Those two houses known by the signs of "The Dog" and " The Ship Inn have happily ncw ceased to exist. Is the said door in "Ship-yard" a public requirement— or will it be resorted to, and made use of, by the half- naked men and women, that, as a rule, use back doors, and which the justices of Liverpool are trying to close? They have an idea that it is best for the publican's own Safety to have legitimate and honourable retailing of drink to persons not inebriated. I trust some one will enlighten me as to my enquiry in your next issue, and oblige A WATCH DOG WITHOUT A MUZZLE.

YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION. Sir,—Now that we have entered upon another year, it is to be hoped that the above institution, which is so much needed in Warrington, may meet with greater Success than it has achieved in the past, but it would appear from the tone of the annual meeting held on Tuesday evening that the light of the religious lamp of this association is burning very low. The enthusiasm for worldly amusements is, of course, in the ascendancy, as manifested by the glowing reports of the various se- cular clubs with which the association abounds. Where • was the repo: of the Evangelistic services, which are,or Should be, held on Sundays similar to those conducted by kindred associations? In vain did the meeting look for this, and the enquiry by the chairman for such re- port, elicited no satisfactory response. It was, cer- tainly, a matter of regrc*., that the most important re- presentatives of the committee were absent ; and also that some of the most zealous workers who identified themselves with the spititual work of the association have recently resigned for some apparently unexplained reason. I hope,however,that the new;committee will prove even more enthusiastic than the gentlemen referred to in sup- porting the Christian work which was so successfully begun at the old premises in Bold-st.—l am, Sir, yours faithfully,
JOHN E. HISLOP. 79, Manchester-road, Warrington, January 14th, 1892.

MELTING SNOW IN TIIE STREETS. Sir,—There has been, this winter, the usual crop of inventors who, without the slightest knowledge of the subject they advocate, endeavour to enlist the time and money of others, as ignorant as themselvles, in a very foolish scheme, i.e., to use ordinary gas to melt the snow which pbstructs the streets, some of the sanguine having gone to some expense in demonstrating what was already known, i.e., the possibility of it irrespective of Cost. How absurd such a project is can be easily seen by comparing the known heating value of coal gas with the work to be done. Six inches deep of averaae snow, when melted, becomes half an inch depth of water, 24 square feet of which will weight 62ilbs., or 23.41bs per square yard. At this rate the snow on one mile (or 1,760 yards) of a street 20 yards wide would, if 6in. deep, weigh $23,6801b5. or 363 i tons. The heating power of London gas is 660 units per cubic foot, Le., one cubic foot of coal gas will heat
6601b5. of water ldeg. Fahrenheit, and this we may take it as a maximum that 500 units could be utilized

It has been proved repeatedly and beyond question that 11b. of snow at freozing point requires 150 units of heat to melt it and raise the temperature of the water obtained to 40 deg. Fahrenheit, and this effect would be produced on 3ilbs. of snow by the consumption of one cubic foot of coal gas. From the above data it will be found that to melt the snow in the assumed naile of street would require the consumption of two hundred and forty seven thousand cubic feet of gas, costing, 3s. per 1,000 cubic feet, a iittle over £37, er at the rate of £3,256 per square mile. . .

-- As there are a great many square miles of streets in many towns, and as the snowfall has already been nearly double that assumed, it will be seen that the problem is, most certainly, not one to be solved by this method. Even if we were to assume that the cost of gas and labour was not prohibitive, the fact that the ground itself is usually colder than 32 deg. must be considered, and the ground would also have to be warmed,or a thin surface ot glassy ice, of the most slippery and dangerous kind, would remain after the snow was removed ; this alone would condemn the project as being unworthy of consideration.
THOMAS FLETCHER, F.C.S.
Warrington. THE DOCTRINE OF EVOLUTION.

Sir,—Mr. Peers gives himself away in every paragraph of his last letter, and this as a matter of simple critic- ism. lam not disposed to take advantage of his weak- ness. Abiogenesis " has not a single fact to support it," but Mr. Peers has an unbiassed belief in it notwithstand- ing ; unbiassed by contrary facts, I suppose he means. He is quite right; the probabilities are dead against the doctrine of the evolution of life, and wholly in favour of the spiritual origin of that mystical and wonderful force which has silently built up the elaborate structure of living nature. The doctrine of the spiritual origin of life uproots atheistic evolution, breaks Spencer's philo- sophy of the Unknowable in two, discredits Tynds.ll's poetical conception of Matter, and paves the way to a better appreciation of the fact that God has not left him- self in this materialistic age without a witness, power- ful and incorruptible. There is to be no discussion of abiogenesis then : the case goes by default. Mr. Peers would like me to " champion" " Metho- doxy." Now, " Methodoxy," like the term which ex- presses it, is a creation of Mr. Peers's imagination. Not my views but his own are at stake, and on second thought, I accept his challenge to discuss with him the origin of man. But one or two things remain to be said. Firstly, the origin of man is one thing, and the relation of that origin to current religious belief, or to the alleged teaching of the Bible, is quite another. The former is a scientific and the latter a theological question. It is the former question we are to discuss—that is to say the doctrine of man's development from the brute. When that is finished, if a long-suffering Editor will permit, I shall have no objec- tion to discussing the theological aspect of the case. If Mr. Peers sees and appreciates the distinction here drawn between the scientific and theological sides of the pro- posed discussion, then your readers may look forward to next week for a carefully developed argument in favour of man's gradual ascent from primitive animalism. Such aa argument shall have my closest attention, and I will undertake to build up a counter position. Secondly,—No new matter to be introduced in the last letter of each writer ; and further the suggestien, made in all candour, that satirical headlines will be out of place the next few weeks.—l am yours truly, W. H. BUTLER. Wilderspool.

THE ILLEGAL USE OF OWN LIFE POLICIES. Sir,— I shall be thankful to you, if you would grant me a further favour,by insertion of the following remarks on the above subject, feeling sure also, that by so doing, you will earn the gratitude of such of your readers as have suffered loss, vexation and trouble, and also of those, who, being forewarned, will be able to shun the temptation of entering those persons they have no rights to assure, and to shun those policies which are nothing more nor less than gigantic frauds. I am desirous of dealing principally with the question of own life policies on the life of another person i.e. (a policy with only one name on, where another person pays the premium from the commencement). This question is of vital importance to the readers of your valuable paper. It is also of vital importance to the true interests of every life company, or society, and the interests of the honest members, who make honest contracts and pay their honest pounds, shillings, and pence. This I system permeates the whole land from Cornwall to the Scottish coast, gambling and speculating in human 1 beings, as so many cattle. I unhesitatingly affirm that this adulteration of the insurance business is mainly, or partially, caused, by, carried on by, and secretly covered and encouraged by the use and the abuse of own life proposals and own life policies. And who can be responsible for this system, but those who deal them out ? Either the agent, super- intendent, or the office, must certainly be held respon- sible for their use in the majority of cases. Although I am connected with the Industrial Branch in a respon- sible position, I cannot view this mode of corrupt deal- ing without knowing what influence this system exer- cises upon men, who desire to do well to bring fair con- tracts to their respective offices. This system has blighted the prospects of thousands of honest artisans, who have entered the profession as agents, only to leave in disgust or discharged for pursu- ing a course marked out by others, or have, perchance remained, and become hardened to intrigues that would be scorned in any respectable trading concern. lam fairly convinced that the outlook is gloomy indeed, with a continuance of their mode of canvassing and obtaining new business, for those new beginners who start with a clear book, a clear conscience. Bad contracts, and bad contractors, ought to be chiselled out—as rotten bricks from a good building, for I consider every policy issued, as so many bricks, used to build up the edifice of life assurance. It depends upon the quality and not the quantity, and up- on the character of the workmen employed, whether the building stands and endures. I maintain, that it is the duty of the public to begin to learn what are the principles of Insurance. That there is a vast proportion of the population quite ignorant of the insurance laws—need not be disputed, and I would • strongly advise some means whereby the public should • learn more ; upon how they should act to defend them- • selves—and after they have been educated, they would I help officials to do right. If something in this direction 1 is not done the law givers may take the initiative. At the present time, everything is done at random. It , is nobody's duty or interest to prosecute the forgers, or the receiver of monies under false pretences. I would establish a precedent,and invite those who are connected ' with insurance to allow the public to know what is right and what is wrong.—l remain dear sir, yours faithfully, JOHN MOORFIELD. 44, Parker-st., WaiTington, Jan. 20th, 1592.

THE EARLESTOWN PUBLIC HALL QUESTION. Sir,—l am disposed to think the Earlestown people are inclined to be somewhat jealous of Newton, and as regards Mr. Ratcliffe and other property owners near to the proposed Public Hall it may be that this is mixed up with a little selfishness. lam simply a working-man, a constant reader of the Examiner," wishful to learn all I can about local matters, and with your permission, Mr. Editor, I will place before your readers my views on the matter. _ _ _

Mr. Legh very kindly offered to give £5OO for a park to the town (it was to the whole town and not Earles- town only) which would have been for the benefit of all the inhabitants. The Earlestown people said—" No, we want no park, we will ask Mr. Legh to give the £5OO to- wards a Public Hall," which I understeod he agreed to do. The hall at Earlestown can benefit the Newton people in no way whatever, yet the latter without a murmur, in their desire to be agreeable and neighbourly, gave up their right to their portion of Mr. Legh's gift of £5OO, as they did not object to Earlestown having a hall in which to hold their public meetings, and the cost agreed on was £5,000. But the Commissioners, having got in the thin end of the wedge, decided on their own authority, without con- sulting the ratepayers, to increase the contract price to £7,700, which actually means £lO,OOO to £15,000, when 1 all the extras, and the annual expenditure on the build- ing capitalized are included. They said they would not only have a hall for public meetings, but have the offices there also. From my humble point of view the present Commissioners have exceeded their powers. Morally at any rate they have broken faith with the ratepayers. The correspondence in the papers has enlightened your humble servant, and I know it has had a similar effect on others, but more information is yet required. I want o know are the Commissioners to override their constituents in this high-handed manner ? Is there no remedy ? Are we workingmen to allow ourselves to be gulled? What is Mr. Stewart doing? He is in the running as a candidate at the next election and under- stands law. Why does he not come forward and help? He has such a chance to distinguish himself that he may never have the like again. But I wish to refer to my own case; my rent is ss. per week, and lam told the assesment is £9. I live out- side the charmed circle of the Town Hall site and the hall will be of no use to me. My landlord said to me— " These foolish Commissioners are going to put up a large and expensive building at Earlestown, which woald increase the rates perhaps to the extent of is. in the £ or more, and if that takes place, your rent will be ss. 3d. instead of 55., and he had no doubt the rent of a cottage tenant, would be increased every working-man, proportionately. These working-men agitators never made a greater mistake if they imagined they were to have a public hall without money out of pocket. I am glad to see in one of the letters that the Local Government Board is to be consulted. It is not too late. We all remember what the late Dan O'Connell said—
-NAk
