div.head: EXAM INER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 23, 1892,
div.p: THE EXAM INER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 23, 1892,

" A coach and four could be driven through any Act of Parliament." If the inhabitants desire it, the Commis- sioners can be pulled up in their reckless career. Have a public meeting by all means ; get up a monster petition; forward it to the Local Government Board, and ask for an Inspector to be sent down to have a general enquiry. The agitators for the Public Hall have not come forward to support their actions by arguments and why? They dare not : their case is rotten to the core ; and for the people to allow themselves to be hoodwinked by Blue Bottleism is beyond my comprehension. Only one letter has appeared in support of the action of the Commis- sioners—that of" Artizan," and and he brings out quite a novel idea. "The old dingy Petty Session Court Room, at Newton, which has served as a Town Hall &c. for the last generation, might serve the inhabitants of Newton-le- Willows, but it is not the sort of thing that will suit the fastidious taste of Earlestown people." It would be a good way of comparing the taste of the Earlestown with the Newton people by the Commis- sioners they elect. I will not mention names ; all know them, and will form their own opinion of " Artizan's " production. One thing I am quite sure of ; I will not pay 3d. per week extra if I can help it, to make the interested part- ies richer or to met the Earlestown people's " fastidious tastes ;" and I now call upon all my comrades in labour to help to upset what appears to me to be one of the most abominable proceedings of our time. A WORKING-MAN. January 18 1892.

"Iv yo' want to know the time "—hear Dr. Parker. . .

Lie's bin givin a lectnre on clocks an' watches, an' lettin' fooak know th' time o' day—an' that's wod they want to know neawadays when there's Bich misleeadin timepieces i' th' merkut. Aw hooap th, Doctor compared his werkin'-men audience—iv ony werkin'-men could affoord th' cherge med to hear him—to clocks an' watches; he could tell 'em heaw fast some on 'era wor, an' heaw slow others ; heaw a lot o' " hands" wodu'd gooa on strike, or, as like clocks, they wodn'd strike till they were forced—an' nod olez then. Aw'm a bloodthirsty humourist, aw am! Then he could show as they gooa on "tick " mooastly—lust like clocks, an' through gooin' on tick they want " winding up" neaw an' ageean; see thad ? An' like clocks they want regulatin'. But wod abeawt th' main spring breykin' ? Well, aw hooap th' Doctor showed 'em "what a piece of work is a man! how noble in reason ! how infinite in faculty! in form and motion how express and admirable ! in action, how like an angel! in apprehension, how like a god! the beauty of the world ! the paragon pf animals !" (Good owd author o' Shakespare's werks !) Th' comparison ends when yo' come to consider th' wonderful thing a human eye is. "The spheri- cal eyeball, the lenses with different refracting powe •s, the iris or coloured rim for enabling us to admit or exclude egress of light, by the mysterious provisior for instant focussing." An' yet, heaw thowtlessly some fooak stick their kneyve ageean this worderful object! An' th' kneyve is just as wonderful, mind yo', an' th' ear, an' lungs. But wod abeawt tiled main spring breykin' ? Nowt. Id isn'd my bizness ; it's moore i' Dr. Par- kei's line. •Onybody knows as th' main spring ov a watch con burned reight for varry little bi tekkin' id to a watchmekker—or for less by a blacksmith, as Mark Twain fun eawt to his cost. But this main- spring to this wonderful piece o' mechanism co'd Man—!

Good news for werkin' *men ! No moore strikes! No moore injustice ! No moore sweeatin' I No moote lockeawts, etsettera. Wad is th' remedy, yo ax? Givin' o'er werkin' ? Nowe, though thad wod mend things, an' id isn'd a good thing werkin' between meals. Id seems as th London Chamber o' Commerce is organisin' a Con- ciliation Booard "to promote amicable methods of settling disputes, and the prevention of strikes and lockouts." No less nor sixty trade unions belong to th' Booard, an' bi sendin' delegates to th' meetin's th' men come f contact wi' th' employers ; there's " perfect equality of representation end voting power," an' id seems as this feature hes werkt weel i th' settlement o' questions browt afore th' Booard. Some o'th' Chambers o' Commerce i' th' provinces hey these Conciliation.Booards gooin', all' th' noos- pappers are recommendin' th' others to follow suit. Afoore, aw korroborated aw should like to see id werk ; an' aw suppoose id'll be a case o' droppin' so mich th' slot fost. Well, they mast hey a spell at th' Bromsgrove Nailmekkers dispute to begin wi' * *
Just a word or two on Sales _an' "Sells."

Iv there's one thing i' o' th' world as wimmen like—ay, an' men too—but moore especially wim' men—it's mekkin' bergains : they'll gooa ceawerin- o' day at a sale room to save a penny, when they owt to be at hooam darnin' th' childer's stockin's or stitchin' buttons on their husbands shirts or breeches Like as iv its born i' mooast folk to want to get a sixpenny article for a penny ; they ne'er think, or keer, whooa loyses fippence on id, an' as often as nod—a lot oftener—they ged suckt in. Chaps'll speculate i' things they're nod pertick- lerly i' want on when they'er mekkin' a snap ; hap- pen it's an owd sailor (?) as hes some smuggled silk hankitchers wo'th five shillin' apiece, to sell at ninepence ; or a bit o"bacca as hes ne'er paid duty' (for a varra good reason) to sell at a shillin' at hofe a peawnd; or a good lookin stick—a Malacca—for a tanner. Deawn gooas th' brass, an' when th' chap shows his wife the hankitchers hoo tells him as they're nobbut cotton one way an' summat else t'other way, an' as its dear at thrippence ; same wi' th' cheeap 'bacca—it's ayther cabbige, lettice, or tay leeaves ; th' grand walkin' stick torns eawt to be pipeclay. Th' wimmen thersel's is no better, for they'll buy ony mortal thing i' th' bergain line ; they co' id savin' a bit ce summat. Wor id Professor Iluxley as.med thad big scientifick discovery as one penny tin pepperbox 'ill last a big family three score year an' ten, even iv it's i' regular use? Well, id doesn'd matter whooa id wor, becose id doesn'd stop a woman fro' buyin' thirteen on 'ern for a shillin' simply becose hoo geds th' odd un chuckt in as a bergain. But this isn'd th' wost specimen o' their economical werk, for yo may send 'em to a auction- room wi nobbut hofe a creawn i' their pockets, an' abeawt four or five heawrs at after they'll come lorryin' hooam wi' th' followin':— A clock; A pair of ballies ; An umbrell ; A pair of boots; A sauce pon; An' thrippence change! Yo' wondor heaw the hangmut hoo's done id, an' at fost yo' nobbut keer to know as hoo hes done id' someheaw, an' then when yo've examined th' ber- gains yo' begin to see heaw hoo hes "done id an' yo' wish as hoo hedn'd. Fost ov o' yo' find as th' clock hes imitated thad as yo' read abeawt th' song bi stoppin' short ne'er to gooa ageean ; yo' give a clock-doctor sixpence for boilin' id, an' as thad does no good yo' tek id to a jeweller, an' he charges goodness knows heaw mich. Th' ballies hes chronic congestion o' th' lungs, but yo're wife sets to werk to raise th' wind wi' a stockin' needle an' some wustid ; th' cobbler hes to petch 'em up at th' finish, an' he cherges as mich as iv he'd soyl'd a pair of shoon. Yo' find as th' umbrell hes some compeawn fractures o' th' ribs, wants a fresh stick, an' re- coverin' ; as th' pair o' shoon is ayther booath lefts or booath reights—au' yo' con fancy wod id wod cost to advertise i' th' pappers for the mon as bed t' other two lefts or reights. An' th' wost' thing ov o' wod be to find as th' sauce-pon bed a little hoyle th' bottom on 't, for yo've never done hevin' th' plumber i' th' heawse to soder that.pon ; a plumber con spend hofe-a-day at onytime petchin' up a little hoyle wi' rosin' an' lead. Iv yo'ra one o' them chaps as books o' these things deawn in a diary yo'll find as this grand bergain 'll cost abeawt two peawnd --in fact thad sum wod ha' bowt 'em new fro' a good shop, an' fro' a hire system shop they wodn'd ha' cost mich moore nor four peawnd. It's a good owd sayin' an' a true un is thad abeaw` bein'
Penny wise an' peawnd foolish. * *

The New Year geds woss as id geds owder, an' there's no varra breet eawtlook yet, as far as aw con see. Last week were a sad week, wod wi' th' young Prince an' Cardinal Manning deein'; this week th' pappers are full o"lection news abeawt Rossendale—an' thad interests me varra little. Aw see Stepniak were at Manchester last Tuesda', an' lectured on th' famine i' Russia; he showed as th' Emperor said there were no famine, an' that's nerance. Id wur but t'other week as th' Empress hed a present ov a fur clooak as cost a tooathri theawsand peawnd, an' iv aw were i' hor place, an' knew o'th' sad state o' things, aw'd pop that clooak an' gi' th' brass to th' relief fund. But we corn'd see eawrsels as others see Us; we tawk o' things bein' bad here i' England one day, an' th' next we raise a hunderd theawsand for Booth to mek things woss wi'. Ov cooarse th' Russians are enemies, an' Stepniak's right abeawt enmity endin' an' human- ity beginnin' ; but it's herd lines to be axt to put ' summat i'th' hat when we're towd heaw heavily taxed th' poor fooak are, an as • that's th' cause o' o'th' poverty. Well, it's better bein' a bit too soft nor a bit too herd, an' a chap is herd as con be unmoved at th' idea o' theavvsands o'wi mmen an' childer bein welly clamed to death—to say nowt o'th' men. Be gene- rous, iv they hey sent us th' inflooenza two year I together.

div.head: DEATH OF A CENTENARIAN.
div.p: DEATH OF A CENTENARIAN.

Betty Joce, an inmate of the South Molton Union Workhouse, Devon, died on Thursday morning at the age of 106 years. Although she had been bed-ridden for the past few months she retained her faculties to the last She was a native of South Molton.

div.head: ROSSENDALE ELECTION.
div.p: ROSSENDALE ELECTION.

Sir Thomas Brooks (Unionist) and Mr. John Henry Maden (Liberal) were duly nominated at Bacup on Tues- day as candidates for the parliamentary representation of Rosseadale. Sir T. Brook's agent deposited 20 nomination papers, including one from the Conservative exclusively and another from Liberal Unionists. Mr. Maden's agent put in twelve papers. One of these was an Irish nomination, and another contained the names of ex-Liberal Unionists. The election takes place to-day (Saturday). Mr. Mader) received on Tuesday evening a letter from Mr. Gladstone, in which the ex-Premier recalls that Lord Hartington in 1886 promised the large introduction into the Irish Government of the representation prin- ciple and a fundamental reform in the system known as Duiplin Castle. Instead of the fulfilment of thesepledges, Ireland has been placed undera law of perpetual coercion and the credit of the Exchequer had been pledged to the extent of a hundred millions for the purchase of Irish estates. The Government claims to have done more than any other to alienate the Irish from the British people and dishonour the name of law and order. Six Unionist meetings were held in the Rossendale division on Thursday night. The Liberals had a tinal meeting in the Haslingden Public Hall, at which Mr. T. P. O'Connor, M.P., and Mr. Lloyd George, M.P.. were the chief speakers. Mr. Madan was unfortunately still unable through, indisposition to be present. The meet- ing was crowded to excess, and enthusiastic through- out.
FATALITIES ON THE SHIP CANAL.

Mr. Yates held two inquests at Latchford Hospi- tal yesterday. The first was on the death of John Donlan, fireman, 9, Naylor-street, Warrington, who was killed at Rixton Leys, on Wednesday morning. The deceased's sister and her brother had on two previous occasions complained of the tubes on his engine twisting. Henry Lewis, driver of the engine, said that one of the tubes burst, as they were taking trucks of sand up an incline. Witness stuck to the engine, but deceased and the rope runner jumped off. The deceased's body was found in the four- foot way, on its side quite dead and shockingly mangled. About two months ago a tube burst and the deceased jumped off then, but received no injury. The engine had been examined on that occasion. Smith, the rope-runsier, gave corrobora- tive evidence. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death." A MAN KILLED AT ACTON GRANGE. The other inquest was on the body of Robert Marshall, about twenty-two years of age, belong- ing to the Bridgeton Division of Glasgow, a painter on the bridge at Acton Grange, near Warrington, who was killed there on Thursday.—James Forbes, from Aberdeen, a fellow-workman, said the deceased stepped on to a plank, slipped from the girder, and fell a distance of 20ft. alighting on his head. The workmen were leaving off for breakfast, and de- ceased was crossing the staging to the ladder. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.
PARR'S BANKING COMPANY, LIMITED,
ANNUAL BALANCE SHEET.

In the report which they had issued to the share- holders the directors of Parr's Banking Company state that they have to report that the position and prospects of the business continue to be in every way satisfactory. By the issue of 2,500 new shares in terms of resolution passed on 24th July, and confirmed on 21st August last, the subscribed cap- ital has been increased from £3,000,000 to .£3,250,000, the paid up capital from .£600,000 to £650,000, and the reserve fund from £370,000 to .£377,400. The transference of Messrs. Furer, Banbury, Nix and Company's business to this bank has been satisfac- torily completed. The registered office of the Com- pany has been transferred to 77 Lombard-st., Lon- don. Including .£27,206 4s. Sd. brought from previ- ous account, the net balance of profits,aft provid- ing amply for all bad and doubtful debts, and rebating the current bills at five per cen ~, is .£164,491 7s. 10d. The dist*ibution of this sum, re- commended by the directors,is as follows :—lnterim half year's dividend of 91 per cent., declared 24th July £57,000, dividend to be now paid of 9i per cent., free of income tax .£61,750, to write down to 90 consols recently purchased .£2,780 17s. 6d., to reserve F.. d—raising it to .£390,000 .£12,600, to property account .£2,500, balance to next account £27,860 108. 4d.,tothl £164,491 7s. 10d. The directors record with deep regret the death of their esteemed colleagues, Mr. Thomas Philip Parr and Mr. Henry Woodcock.

"No ADMITTANCE EXCEPT ON BUSINESS." Last evening week, in connection with the Wes- leyan Band of Hope, a lecture, entitled " No admit- tance -cept on business," illustrated by experi- ments, specimens, and diagrams, was given in the- Wesleyan Day school by Mr. J. J. Jakeman, school lecturer of the Liverpool Temperance Band of Hope Union. Owing to the inclement weather there was only a poor attendance. Mr. R. E. Garnett occupied the chair and introduced the lecturer. The lecture was most ably given, and was attentively listened to. The meeting closed by singing the Doxology. ST. MARY'S SUNDAY SCHOOLS. Yesterday afternoon week the annual tea party and prize distribution in connection with the Sankey and Penketh branches of the St. Mary's Church Sun- day Schools was held in the Sunday Schools, Great Sankey. The tea was prepared and the tables pre- sided over by the lady tea,diers of the school, and all the children did full justice to the good fare pro- vided. After tea,the rc 3131 was re-arranged, ann an entertainment given, the programme being contri- buted by the teachers and friends. At the close of the entertainment,the prizes for regular attendance 4lrc., were given, most of the scholars receiving a present of some description DEATH OF MR. T. HUGHES. It is with regre., that we record the death of Mr. T. Hughes, of Great S nkey, which took place sud- denly yesterday week, at his residence, Fern Lea. The deceased, who was a Wesleyan local preacher on the plan of the Warrington circuit, was highly respected by all who knew him, and his death is much mourned. Owing to age and increasing infir- mities, Mr. Hughes has seldom appeared in public of late years. Mr. Hughes had reached the age of 72. The death was reported to the coroner, who notified the registrar (Mr. B. Hobson) that he did not think it necessary to hold an inquest. The cause of death was failure of the heart's action. The in- terment took place on Tuesday at Warrington Ceme- tery.

div.head: UNION [ST DEMONSTRATION AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: UNION [ST DEMONSTRATION AT EARLESTOWN.

SPEECHES BY LORD CASTLETOWN, COLONEL BLUNDELL, M.P., AND MR. T. W. LEGH, M.P. On Thursday evening last a demonstration of Unionists was held in the Viaduct Institute, Bayles- town. Mr. T. H. Pearson, J.P., presided, and amongst others on a full platform were Lord Castle- town, Col. Blundell, M.P., Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P., Dr. Beaman. Mr. T. D. Grimke-Drayton, Mr. W. Robinson, Rev. J. Carson (NV inwick), Mr. W. H. Brooke (Warrington), Mr. C. B. F. Borron, Mr. J. Fairclough, Mr. J. E. Pardey, Dr. Street, Mr. J. W. Thorpe, Mr. R. Bradshaw, Mr. R. H. Wright, Mr. J. Warburton, Mr. J. Catherall, Mr. A. Jackson, Mr. W. Houghton, &c. There was a large attendance. The Chairman said the time was not far distant when they would be called upon to recoid their votes between two candidates, and he thought their choice would not be a very difficult one. Their member was a tried man ; they all knew him ; was always ready to come amongst them, and always ready to be of service to any of his constituents. (Hear, hear.) He also supported a Government which had always been, so successful in all it had undertaken. (Applause.) Mr. C. B. F. Herron moved the following resolution : " That the meeting desires to record its full confidence in the Unionist Government and congratulates Her Majesty's ministers on their successful home and foreign policy,and trusts that the beneficient legislation already eaected and nolV being proceeded with will secure the continued union and prosperity of the nation." (Ap- plause.) Mr. Grimke-Drayton seconded the resolution. He said that so far as the Unionist Government was concerned he thought it had given them all that they wanted and all that they asked for. Of course there were a few vision- ary things they had not given them, such as the equal division of property amongst all men, and thus ruining the country and making all men poor, but he hoped the Government would never give them that. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P. who was received with loud applause, said tnere had lately occurred an incident in that division which had led to an increase of political excitement. He need hardly say that he alluded to the appearance of a Liberal candidate. That was an event for which they had waited for a long time. For his own part he did not look upon it as so entirely a disagreeable incident in political life as some of them might imagine, because, at any rate, for one thing it gave them some- thing fresh to talk about. He observed that the Liberal candidate—a gentleman, by the way, of whom he heard an excellent account—had a spirit not commonly found amongst Liberal candidates, namely,a spirit of modesty. He inferred this from an account he read of Mr. Neill's reception at Earlestown. He alluded to the fact that he had no local recommendation, and he was of opinion that a local man would carry more weight and more support than a person imported from outside. In his (Mr. Legh's) opinion that spoke volumes for the difference between the Unionist and Gladstonian party at the present moment. There in that room they had seen representatives of the working classes, representatives of the landlords, representatives of most of the professions, and they had seen nearly all the most prominent employers of labour in that district —all these they had seen in that room in support of the Unionist cause. It said much, therefore, for the differ- ence which existed between the Gladstonian and the Unionist cause, that the Liberal party in the division were unable to produce a local man. (Hear, hear and applause.) It only showed the effect that the Home Rule heresy had produced upon their party. (Hear.. hear.) With regard to the last election he was told that he did himself a great deal of harm by excessive modesty. He was not going to fall into that mistake this time. (Laughter and applause.) He would, there- fore, take the earliest opportunity of asserting that, he was, in his own opinion, just as well qualified to repre- sent them as Mr. Neill. (Applause.) But he must add this. If they were going *to depend upon promises there was no comparison between him and Mr. Neill. He would like to point out that they Unionists did not claim their support upon what they were disposed to give them if they continued in office. What they did claim their support for was their conduct during the time they had been in office. (Applause.) When he thought of what had been done for the country by the present Government during the past five years, he often wondered what woul* be the language of their °poo- -1 nents if they had done all these things. (Hear, hear.) The Unionist Government, so far as was humanly pos- sible, had fulfilled their pledges, and that in the face of the most unscrupulous opposition that any Government had had to encounter. (Hear, hear.) Were the performances of the Unionist Govern- ment, were the benefits which they had enjoyed at their hands, to be entirely forgotten in consequence of the illusory promises which were made to them in the so- called Newcastle programme. He would say of the Newcastle programme that, in his opinion, it was drawn up with a great deal of skill because it appealed to many people and to many sects. It reminded him, however, very strongly of a very old conjuring trick, for no matter what card they selected the Home Rule card would be thrust upon them. What had amused him to a certain extent was Mr. Neill's reference to Home Rule. He said in a somewhat artless manner that lie was under the impression that it was a subject in which his audience took no interest. He (Mr. Legh) would ask them if it had come to that ? Had the union of hearts, the visits of Gladstonian members to Ireland, Ireland's agony and all that, had it COMB to this, that a Gladstonian candidate had to appear before a meeting and confess that he was under the impression that Home Rule possessed no interest. Could anything show more distinctly the sham of the whole thing. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He believed that the realisation of Home Rule hopes was much farther off now than it was when the present Government came into office. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The next election would be largely contested upon the eight hours ques- den, and in all probability they should hear consider- ably about the eight hours question than about the Irish question. He declined to discuss a general eight- hours bill altogether, because he believed it to be wholly impracticable, and ,‘ the fact that it was distinctly impracticable was even admitted by the present Liberal candidate for the division The proposition that concerned them more particularly was that with reference to the eight hours bill for miners. He had been, during the last few years, frequently urged to support a measure forbidding colliers to work more than eight hours, but he bad always resisted that appeal. At the same time he must admit that probably in the opinion of many people he was committiwa a great tacti- cal mistake. But, although he had been engaged for five or six years in politics, he had not been so entirely demoralised yet that he was prepared to support a mea- sure simply because it would bring in a certain number of votes. (Applause.) It seemed to him that the argu- ments against the Bill were considerably more potent than those advanced in favour of it, and therefore he had not the slightest intention of voting for it. (Hear hear and applause.) Colonel Blundell, M.P., also dealt with the question of an Eight Hours Bill for miners. The advocates of the Bill based many of their arguments on the idea that the calling of the miner was an unhealthy one, but ac- cording to the figures showing the relative death-rates, the coalminer had a better expectation of life than the man who walked in the streets. The miner. in fact, had a better expectation of life than the general body of I those who were not miners. He ventured to think a ' hard and fast limit of eight hours a day.was impractic- able. He believed it would be bad for the country and bad for everybody concerned, and it ought not to come into force. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Lord Castletown,who wassOceived with loud applause, said the issue of the next election would turn practically on the question of Home Rule, and if the Liberals were returned to power Mr. Gladstone would so warp his cabinet to Home Rule, that all the great social questions would be shelved. The late Mr. Par- nell had always insisted upon the right of the Irish Parliament to the complete control of the new police forces in Ireland. Mr. Parnell never did a thing and never wrote a thing without a deep ulterior object, and his object in this case was what he (Lord Castle- town) knew it to be. The moment an Irish Parliament was created the police force now in existence was to be disbanded. A new force would then be created. There would be no difficulty about recruits for thousands of Irishmen would comefrom America, and thousands of Fenians from different parts of Ireland would join. The result would be that there would be aa organised armed force in Ireland owing allegiance to a supposed subordinate Parliament, and ready at a moment to do what they were told to do by their Irish ministers. Were they to have within two hours of their shores an island filled with mercenaries and auxiliaries from America, and a home for all their toes? ("No," and applause.) In conclusion,Lord Castletown said that an election would soon take place. They had their own' social questions which required settlement ; let them see that they were settled, and settled by a Unioniet Government. Flame Rule was not wanted for either Ireland or England, it was not good for either of them, ' and it was not required by the justice of, the case. (Loud applause.) The resolution was then put to the meeting arid car- ried unanimously. s On the motion of Mr. J. Wright, the followinss resolu- tion was also passed s---" That this meeting tenders to Mr.T. W. Legh a hearty vote of thanks for his services in Parliament, with the assurance of continued confidence and support." The meeting concluded with the usual votes of thanks., -.maw

The Marquis of Lorne is gasetted governor and con- stable of Windsor Castle. Another fall took place on Thursday night in the Wor- cester Railway Tunnel, injuring four workmen.

ROYAL VISIT TO THE MEMORIAL CHAPEL. Yesterday the Prince of Wales,the Duke of Edinburgh, and the Grand Duke Alexis visited the Memorial Chapel at Windsor, and afterwards left for town. MR. HASTINGS J.P., COMMITTEE FOR TRIAL. At Bow-street, on Friday, Mr. Hastings, M.P., was charged on remand, with misappropriating £15,000 of which he was trustee under th& will of the late Majoy John Brown. The accused seemed very depressed. Evidence having been given, the accused was committed for trial at the Old Bailey, bail being fixed at £lO,OOO and two sureties of £5,000 each. Application to reduce bail was refused, and accused was removed in castody. DOUBLE MURDER AND° SUICIDE.

The Press -Association's Nottingham correspondent telegraphs :--A shocking tragedy has been enacted here, Mary Ann Castings, widow, aged 32', having killed her two children, Emily, aged 10, and Ernest Stanley, aged 8, and then committed suicide by cutting her throat. The poor children had their heads battered in with a coal hammer, and Mrs. Castings, who kept a milliner's and haberdasher's shop in one of the principal thorough- fares ef Nottingham, cut her throat with a razor. No motive is assigned for the crime. Later inquiries show that Mrs.Castings':shop remained closed from Saturday night unril Thursday night, when the police forced the doors.
HOSPITAL BURNT DOWN IN AMERICA. MANY LIVES LOST. NEW Yoßs, FRlDBY.—Nineteen bodies have already been recovered from the still smouldering ruins of the burnt-down Surgical Hospital of Indianopolis.

CONCERT.—A miscellaneous concert was given in the Parochial Schools on Monday evening, the proceeds of which were to go to the new uniform fund of the Lymm Parish Church Brass Band. WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—The usual meeting of the above society was held in the schoolroom on Monday evening. A very interesting paper on " Daniel a true type of of character" was gone through, and ably discussed by various members. Mr. Briggs was in the chair. SoCIM TEA MEETING.—The annual social tea :meeting of the members and friends of the Lymm Congregational Church took place on Tuesday. About 220 sat down to an excellent repast, which was served by the teachers of the Sunday school, the lady members of the congrega- tion waiting at the tables. After tea an entertainment took place, presided over by the pastor,the Rev. C. Clay. who was supported by the Rev. Joseph Johnson, of Ashton-on-Mersey ; Rev. J. Beddell, Mr. Dutton,. and other gentlemen, all of whom gave short addresses.

div.p: CADISHEA.D

TEMPERANCE MEETING.—A public meeting was held in the Cadishead Wesleyan Schoolroom, on Saturday even- ing. The meeting was fairly well attended. Addressess were delivered by Mr. Firth, of Manchester, and Messrs,. Gritnwade and Hawthorne. The Rev. B. Yatespresided over the meeting. A collection was made. SHIP CANAL. MISSION HALL.—A magic lantern enter- tainment was given in this place, on Monday evening_ The subjects for the evening were "Lady Brassey's voyage round the world in the Sunbeam," and also two sets of very interesting slides entitled "The peasant ;: his son, and the ass," and " The maids of Lee." The hall was well filled, and the object—to recompense the care- taker of the hall for het sudden loss—was appreciated. ALLEGED HIGHWAY BOBBERY.—Three labourers,. of Cadishead, named respectively William Hampson, William Hew/ett, and James Occleston,, were charged at the Manchester Gouty Police Court, on Monday morn- ing, before the stipendiary magistrate,. Mr. X. H. P. Leresche, with stealing £3 7s. with violence, from the person of Anton Shepherd a foreigner working on the Manchester Ship Canal. Mr. Bent applied for a remand in consequence of the prosecutor's inability to attend, owing to the prisoners' ill-usage. The remand was granted.

The annual knife-and-fork tea and ball in con- nection with the Warrington branch of the Irish National League was held in the Co-operative Sankey Street, on Tuesday evening. About 150 sat down to tea, being waited upon by the wives of the members of the league. Alter tea dancing was indulged in. An efficient quadrille band.laad been engaged for the occasion, and gave much satisfac- tion to the dancers. Mr. J. Fitzpatrick acted as M.U. The proceedings were concluded about half-past, tyro, on Wednesday morning, by the singing of ". God save Ireland.' NOVEL, READIN.G.—Is IT GOOD OTA BAD?

The above was the subject of an essay read by, Mr. J. Podmore, junior, at the usual weekly meeting of the Wycliffe Young People's Society, on Monday evening, Mr. Ogden presided. The essayist drew attention to the large number of novel readers, men- tioning the fact that over 70 per cent, of the books. borrowed from the Library were novels, and hs.con.- tended that that meant a great waste of time,, and also a bad influence upon the readers. What a. sight waa a novel-reading wife The essayist did not think any person improved his position by reading novels, and said the papers called! Novelettes and the 'Funny Dreadfuls " might well be teamed "the scum of literature." Messrs, Jeffery, Horclen, Wylie, and Ogden, who took past in the discussion, whilst agreeing with the essayist in conderaising such light literature, considered it unworthy to be placed under the head of novels, and were of opinion that much good could be derived from reading such! novels as those written by Dickens, Scott, Rider Haggard, and other good writers. A Tote of thanks to the essayist was proposed by Mr. S. Jeffery, and seconded bx Mr, J, Ball ; and Mr, J, Podmorll sponded.

THE KINGSTON -MILL BRASS BAND. Two sacred concerts were given in the Public Hall on Sunday, afternoon and evening, by the Kingston Mills Brass Band. This band won the gold medal at Belle Vue in 1885-6-7, and the first prize in 1875. They were also first holders of the Samson Fox Challenge Cup, 1890, against all comers and claim to have won over .£3,000 in prizes. In the afternoon the programme included Mendellsohnis "War March of the Priests," a euphonium solo, "There is a green hill far away," by Mr. S. Newton : selection, "Rossini ;" cornet solo, " The [Jost Chord,'' by Mr. W. Smith. concluding with a rendering of the' Hallelujah Chorus." The whole of the pro- pramme was exceedingly well rendered, and the applause of the audience was frequnt and hearty, The evening's programme incinded a chorus from Haydn," The heavens are telling ;" a selection" pati Nachtlager in Granada;" overture, "Poet and peasant, Mr. James Billam ; sad the Festival March,.

Sunday school, but he could tell them that every- thing that could, be done to keep the school ope* had been done, but the Sankey Sugar Works had said, that as the day school was closed, it would be no use to keep the Sunday school together. This' was the first time that he had been refused's/3Y,- thing in connection with the Sunday school,. auu the closing was due in a great measure to the-free Education Bill. He requested the scholars and teachers to attend other schools in the district. Mr. Burrows and others also addressed a few w°,rdoci.3 to those present. The prizes, which consisted or.'" neatly bound volumes, were then presented to the children by Mr. Thompson. The secretary, Burrows,was then presented by Mr. Thompson with a Bible and church services,he having occupied the position for 14 years ;und he suitably acknowledged the gift.

PARR'S BANKING COMPANY, LIMITED. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the Annual Ordinary General Meeting of tins Company will be held at the Bank Premises, Winwick-street. Warrington, on Friday, the 29th day cf January, 1892. at 12 o'clock, for the purpose of declaring a dividend, to be payable on the 2nd February, electing Directors and Auditors, and conducting the Ordinary Business of the Company ; and NOTICE IS HEREBY FURTHER GIVEN, that the Meeting to be held at the time and place aforesaid is also convened as an Extraor- dinary General Meeting, for the purpose of considering, and, If thought expedient, passing the Special Resolution ap- pended hereto, or a Special Resolution to a similar purport or effect, viz. " That the Articles Of Association of the Company be altered by the insertion therein of the following Article, namely "That the alteration made in the Articles of Association by the Special Resolutiots passed on the 24th of July, 1891, and confirmed on the list of August, 1891, with regard to the number of the Select Committee of the Directors shall be amended so as to read as follows :—' The number of the Select Committee of Directors shall for the time being be such number as the Directors may from time to time appoint.'" Should the resolution be passed with or without modifica- tion by the required majority, it will be submitted for confir- mation as a special resolution to a second Extraordinary Meeting, which will be subsequently convened The Transfer Books will be closed from 23rd January to 12th February, both days inclusive. By Order, JOHN DUN, General Manager. 77, Lombard Street, Loudon, 15th January, 1892.
